Case_Content:
Man, 64 years old, no significant medical history, presenting with a left colon tumor revealed by subocclusive syndrome.  Thoraco-abdominal CT scan shows a 6 cm colonic mass and two liver metastases in segments II and V measuring 2.2 and 3 cm. CEA: 120 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, MSS. No extra-hepatic disease.
MDT Discussion: Metastases considered primarily resectable, symptomatic colonic lesion is the priority.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
Reasoning: The liver disease consists of two small (<3 cm) metastases located in segments II and V, which can be removed by limited segmental resections while preserving a large functional liver remnant. No extra‑hepatic disease is present. The primary tumour is symptomatic (obstruction) but the patient has no reported comorbidities that would preclude major abdominal surgery. Although FLR ratio and detailed vascular anatomy are missing, the anticipated resections are minor and, based on standard volumetric expectations, would leave >30 % of liver volume – satisfying the technical criteria for resectability. Therefore surgery can be planned without mandatory pre‑operative down‑staging.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Urgent management of the obstructing left‑colon tumour:  
 – Perform a left‑sided colectomy (segmental resection or left hemicolectomy) with primary anastomosis if intra‑operative assessment deems safe; otherwise create a diverting loop colostomy and plan definitive anastomosis later.  
• Liver surgery:  
 – Because the hepatic resections are limited (segment II and segment V), a simultaneous liver resection can be performed in the same operative session, provided the patient’s physiologic status is acceptable (ASA I‑II, no major cardiopulmonary disease).  
 – If simultaneous resection is deemed too risky (e.g., prolonged operative time, poor intra‑operative condition), stage the procedures: complete the colorectal resection first, allow 2–3 weeks of recovery, then perform the segmental hepatectomies (or combined wedge resections) with intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm margins.  
• Pathology: obtain full histopathologic grading, lymphovascular and perineural invasion status after the primary tumour resection; these data will refine adjuvant recommendations.  
• Adjuvant systemic therapy:  
 – After recovery from surgery (typically 4–6 weeks), initiate standard adjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., 6 months of FOLFOX or CAPOX).  
 – Given RAS‑wild‑type status, add an anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) if the multidisciplinary team judges high‑risk features (poor differentiation, lymphovascular invasion, high CEA).  
• Surveillance: serial CEA measurements and contrast‑enhanced CT (or MRI) of chest/abdomen every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Grade of differentiation of the primary tumour (affects adjuvant therapy intensity).  
• Detailed vascular and biliary involvement of the liver lesions (critical for planning safe hepatic transection).  
• Liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast (provides precise lesion mapping and confirms absence of additional occult metastases).  
• Calculated future liver remnant (FLR) ratio (ensures adequate postoperative liver function).  
• Whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been given (could influence timing of surgery and need for further down‑staging).  
These missing items are the most important to confirm before final operative planning.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with two liver metastases (segments II and V, 2.2 cm and 3 cm), bilobar but peripheral, without radiologic evidence of extrahepatic disease. Both lesions appear technically amenable to limited parenchymal-sparing resections (wedge/segmentectomy) with preservation of adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number, small size, and favorable location of metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Priority: management of the symptomatic primary tumor
• The subocclusive presentation makes the left colonic lesion the immediate priority.
• Perform an oncologic left colectomy first (or ileostomy) with lymphadenectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) to treat the obstruction risk and allow safe continuation of the oncologic strategy.
• Alternative : consider a temporary diversion before colectomy according to exact degree of subocclusion.

B. Early systemic therapy after recovery from colectomy
• After the emergent procedure, perform high-resolution liver MRI to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial anatomy. Precise anatomic mapping is required to avoid intra operative surprise 
• Given the high CEA level (120 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT
• Initiate peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI).
• Given the high CEA level (120 ng/mL), the situation suggests biologically active disease; short-course neoadjuvant therapy allows treatment of micrometastases and assessment of tumor biology.
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy depending on MDT decision and tolerance.

C. Liver surgery after restaging (liver-first not indicated here due to symptoms)
• After 2–3 months of chemotherapy, perform high-resolution liver MRI and CT restaging.
• If stability or response is observed, proceed to parenchymal-sparing liver resections: segment II wedge/segmentectomy and segment V wedge/segmentectomy guided by intra-operative ultrasound.
• Aim for R0 margins (>1mm) while preserving maximal liver parenchyma.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Post-hepatectomy therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including pre-operative cycles).
• Close postoperative surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months given the initially high tumor marker level.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact degree of subocclusion and whether an temporary diversion is required before colectomy.
B. Detailed liver MRI describing vascular and biliary relationships of both metastases to confirm feasibility of parenchymal-sparing resections.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy.
D. Exact location of the left colon tumor (descending vs sigmoid) influencing surgical planning.
E. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA
F. Patient’s nutritional status and postoperative recovery capacity, relevant for timing of chemotherapy.
G. Perform liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 56 years old, incidental discovery of a right colon tumor during a workup for iron deficiency anemia. Thoraco-Abdominal CT scan shows an ileocecal mass and a single 2.5 cm metastasis in segment VI. CEA 35 ng/mL, KRAS mutation present. No other lesions on FDG-PET.
MDT Discussion: Single peripheral metastasis, situation suitable for combined surgical treatment.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront: The liver lesion is solitary (2.5 cm), peripheral (segment VI) and therefore technically amenable to a limited anatomical resection or wedge excision. With only one right‑lobe segment involved, the expected future liver remnant will comfortably exceed the 30 % threshold required for a safe hepatectomy in a normal liver. No extra‑hepatic disease is present. Consequently, curative‑intent surgery can be planned without mandatory pre‑operative down‑staging.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Pre‑operative work‑up – Obtain a contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or CT volumetry) to confirm lesion borders, vascular anatomy and to calculate the FLR ratio; assess the primary tumour for obstruction, perforation or bleeding.  
- Neoadjuvant systemic therapy – Because the disease is resectable but the primary tumour is KRAS‑mutated (anti‑EGFR agents ineffective), give 4 cycles of a fluoropyrimidine‑oxaliplatin doublet (e.g., FOLFOX) combined with bevacizumab. This addresses micrometastatic disease, provides a biologic test of tumour behaviour and aligns with guideline‑recommended peri‑operative chemotherapy for synchronous resectable CRLM.  
- Restaging – Repeat thoraco‑abdominal CT (or MRI) after chemotherapy to verify that the liver lesion remains resectable and that no new lesions have appeared.  
- Surgical sequence – If the primary tumour is asymptomatic (no obstruction, perforation or active bleeding), proceed with a simultaneous operation: right hemicolectomy for the right‑colon primary plus a segment VI resection (or wedge) achieving R0 margins. The combined approach is appropriate because the liver resection is limited and the patient’s performance status is presumed adequate.  
- Post‑operative management – Resume systemic therapy to complete a total of 6 months of peri‑operative chemotherapy (additional 2–4 cycles post‑op). Monitor CEA and schedule surveillance imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- FLR ratio (future liver remnant volume) – needed to confirm that the planned liver resection will leave sufficient functional liver.  
- Liver MRI (or detailed vascular imaging) – required to assess vascular/biliary involvement and arterial anatomy of the segment VI lesion.  
- Status of the primary tumour resection (already resected vs. pending) and any obstructive/bleeding symptoms – essential to decide whether a simultaneous or staged approach is safest.  
- Grade of differentiation of the primary tumour – influences overall prognosis and may affect the aggressiveness of peri‑operative chemotherapy.  
- Confirmation that no systemic therapy has already been administered – to avoid duplicate cycles and to plan the optimal timing of chemotherapy relative to surgery.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient has a single 2.5 cm peripheral metastasis in segment VI, no radiologically evident extra hepatic disease, and the lesion is amenable to a non anatomic wedge resection with an expected R0 margin. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered to be potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI and contrast enhanced CT to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial anatomy. Precise anatomic mapping is required to avoid intra operative surprise.

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) because the tumor is KRAS mutated (no anti EGFR benefit).
• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver MRI (and contrast-enhanced CT).

C. Surgical management
• If restaging confirms continued resectability, perform a simultaneous right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + a segment VI wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. (Simultaneous resection for solitary peripheral metastases is safe and oncologically equivalent to staged procedures 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Alternative : consider two-stage surgical resection of primary and liver tumors / consider right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + an image-guided ablation using high-energy radio waves to generate heat via a probe (if no biliary or large vessels proximity)

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals. A level of 35 ng/mL is acceptable but warrants close surveillance

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy. 
B. Potential extension of primary tumor to adjacent organ (abdominal wall, ureter, small bowel)
C. Detailed vascular/biliary relationship of the liver lesion – essential to confirm that a non anatomic resection will achieve clear margins without compromising hepatic inflow/outflow.
G. Patient’s nutritional status and postoperative recovery capacity, relevant for timing of chemotherapy.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
These items should be obtained before finalizing the operative plan.

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, history of smoking, presenting with T3N1 upper rectal adenocarcinoma with a single 1.8 cm liver metastasis in segment III. Pelvic MRI: limited parietal invasion. CEA 45 ng/mL. RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Single resectable metastasis, possibility of coordinated surgical treatment after short-course radiotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – the solitary 1.8 cm metastasis in segment III is technically amenable to a minor hepatic resection (segmentectomy or wedge) and would likely leave an adequate future liver remnant. However, decisive staging information is missing (no thoraco‑abdominal CT, no liver MRI, no FLR calculation, and no confirmation that there is no extra‑hepatic disease). Because these data are required to confirm oncologic feasibility, resection cannot be offered upfront.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Complete staging work‑up: obtain contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT and liver‑specific MRI (including volumetry) to exclude pulmonary, peritoneal or other distant metastases and to define vascular anatomy and FLR.  
- Initiate short‑course radiotherapy for the upper‑rectal primary (5 × 5 Gy).  
- During the radiotherapy interval give peri‑operative systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6 cycles of FOLFOX; RAS‑wild type permits addition of anti‑EGFR if indicated) to treat micrometastatic disease and to test tumor biology.  
- Restage after chemoradiation: repeat pelvic MRI to assess rectal response, repeat liver MRI/CT to verify that the liver lesion remains ≤2 cm, unchanged or reduced, and that FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % if steatosis).  
- If restaging confirms resectability of both sites, proceed with a simultaneous curative approach: laparoscopic low anterior resection (total mesorectal excision) with a protective loop ileostomy, combined with laparoscopic segment III resection (or non‑anatomic wedge) achieving R0 margins.  
- If the rectal tumor shows excellent response (near‑cCR) and the liver lesion is clearly resectable, a liver‑first strategy (segmentectomy first, then delayed TME) is an alternative, especially if a major hepatectomy were required (not the case here).  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy to complete a total of 6 months systemic therapy (continuing the same regimen used pre‑operatively).  
- Surveillance: CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, CT chest/abdomen‑pelvis or MRI liver every 6 months, and colonoscopic follow‑up per guidelines.

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Thoraco‑abdominal CT scan (to rule out pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic disease).  
- Liver MRI with contrast and volumetric analysis (to confirm lesion characteristics, vascular relationship, and calculate FLR).  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio assessment.  
- Status of primary‑tumor resection (has it already been removed?).  
- Grade of differentiation of the primary tumor (prognostic).  

These items are essential to move from “potentially resectable” to “resectable upfront” and to finalize the surgical plan.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with a single 1.8 cm liver metastasis located in segment III. The lesion seems technically amenable to a parenchymal-sparing resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for solitary, small metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI and contrast enhanced CT to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial liver anatomy. 

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab or cetuximab)
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy depending on MDT strategy.
• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver and rectum MRI (and contrast-enhanced CT) to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control for both

C. Management of the rectal primary (oncologic priority)
• Given the T3N1 upper rectal tumor with limited parietal invasion, long-course radiotherapy is appropriate to optimize local control and allow coordinated surgical planning.

D. Coordinated surgical strategy
• Initiate doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX) during the waiting period following radiotherapy. This period treats potential micrometastatic disease and tests tumor biology.
• Consider image-guided ablation of the single segment III lesion using high-energy radio waves to generate heat via a probe (if no biliary or large vessels proximity)
• After restaging with high-resolution liver MRI and pelvic imaging,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : resection / ablation of the segment III metastasis with follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : resection / ablation of the segment III metastasis followed with strict follow up of primary tumor
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : liver-first resection or ablation of the single segment III metastasis, then rectal resection after appropriate recovery, using a staged or synchronous strategy : oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles).
– Parenchymal-sparing segment III wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins.
Simultaneous resection for solitary peripheral metastases is safe and oncologically equivalent to staged procedures
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge, influencing the type of rectal resection and anastomotic risk.
B. Presence of potential extra-hepatic involvement on 18FDG PET-CT . Chest CT.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
D. Detailed relationship of the liver lesion to segment III vascular structures on liver MRI.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 72 years old, discovery at abdominal CT scan of a transverse colon adenocarcinoma, CEA 410 ng/mL, three liver metastases (segments IV, V and VI) measuring 2 to 3 cm. Liver MRI: partial contact with the right portal branch without invasion. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Primarily resectable metastases, simple liver surgery possible.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The liver lesions are technically resectable (size 2‑3 cm, limited to segments IV, V, VI with only partial contact to the right portal branch and no invasion). However, a decisive piece of information – the future liver remnant (FLR) volume/ratio – is missing, and thoracic imaging to exclude pulmonary metastases is also absent. Both are required to confirm that a safe R0 liver resection leaving adequate functional liver parenchyma is feasible. Until these data are obtained, surgery cannot be performed outright.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy (step‑by‑step)  
• Complete staging: obtain a contrast‑enhanced thoracic CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out lung, bone or brain metastases; perform liver volumetry (CT‑based or MRI‑based) to calculate FLR; review arterial anatomy and portal venous anatomy in detail.  
• If FLR ≥ 30 % (≥ 40 % if chemotherapy will be given) and no extra‑hepatic disease is identified, proceed to the next step. If FLR is insufficient, plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy to augment the remnant.  
• Initiate peri‑operative systemic therapy because the patient has high‑risk features (CEA 410 ng/mL, KRAS‑mutated, synchronous disease). A standard oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX) ± bevacizumab for 3–4 cycles is appropriate; anti‑EGFR agents are not indicated in KRAS‑mutated tumors.  
• Re‑image after chemotherapy to assess tumor response and re‑calculate FLR. If disease remains controlled and FLR is adequate, schedule curative liver surgery: non‑anatomic wedge/segmental resections of segments IV, V, VI aiming for R0 margins, preserving at least two contiguous segments with intact inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  
• Decide sequencing of the primary tumor: the transverse colon lesion is asymptomatic (no obstruction, perforation, or bleeding reported). If the patient’s operative risk is acceptable, a simultaneous right hemicolectomy and liver resection can be performed (liver first, then colon). If the combined procedure is deemed too extensive for a 72‑year‑old, adopt a liver‑first approach: perform hepatic resection, allow recovery (4–6 weeks), then resect the primary colon cancer.  
• Post‑operative management: complete a total of 6 months of peri‑operative chemotherapy (including the pre‑operative cycles) and consider adjuvant oxaliplatin‑based therapy per standard guidelines.  
• Follow‑up: CEA monitoring, cross‑sectional imaging of chest/abdomen every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
• Future liver remnant (FLR) volume/ratio – essential to confirm that a safe hepatic resection can be performed.  
• Thoracic imaging (CT or PET‑CT) – required to exclude pulmonary (or other extra‑hepatic) metastases that would alter the curative intent.  
• Status of the primary colorectal tumor (resected vs. unresected) and presence of obstructive/bleeding symptoms – determines whether a simultaneous or staged approach is needed.  
• Detailed arterial and portal venous anatomy – needed for precise surgical planning and to anticipate need for vascular reconstruction or PVE.  
• Assessment of biliary involvement, necrosis, fibrosis, calcifications, cystic changes, and portal thrombosis – could affect technical feasibility of liver resection.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with three liver metastases located in segments IV, V, and VI (2–3 cm), confined to the right liver and central segments. MRI shows only partial contact with the right portal branch and no evidence of vascular invasion. These lesions appear technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections or anatomicalm resection while preserving adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number and size of metastases with preserved vascular structures, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative systemic therapy (strongly recommended)
• The very high CEA level (410 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation suggest biologically aggressive disease.
• Given the high CEA level (410 ng/mL), perform chest CT scan and high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control according to patient tolerance.
• This allows treatment of potential micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology before surgery.

B. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of the lesions to the right portal branch and confirm maintained resectability.
• Evaluate future liver remnant (FLR) if right hepatectomy of considered.

C. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform combined parenchymal-sparing resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segment IV wedge/segmentectomy.
– Segment V and VI wedge resections.
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Management of the primary tumor
• Transverse colectomy of extended right colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.
• Otherwise, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months given the high CEA level (410 ng/mL).

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Presence of potential extra-hepatic involvement on 18FDG PET-CT and chest CT scan.
B. Detailed vascular mapping on MRI to confirm absence of true portal invasion.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) calculation in case of right hepatectomy.F. Circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI, essential for rectal surgical planning. 
D. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Man, 59 years old, T3N1 sigmoid colon tumor associated with four peripheral liver metastases (segments II, III, V, VIII) at the abdominal CT scan. Maximum size: 2.9 cm. CEA 200 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, HER2 negative.
MDT Discussion: Primarily resectable lesions, no vascular or extra-hepatic involvement.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning:  
- Liver metastases are synchronous, four in number, ≤ 3 cm, located in segments II, III, V and VIII with no vascular contact (Analysis 2‑PresenceOfVascularContactOrInvasion = False).  
- No extra‑hepatic disease is identified on imaging (Analysis 3 all “False” except brain = Missing).  
- Technical criteria for resection (ability to preserve ≥ 2 contiguous segments, maintain inflow/outflow and biliary drainage) appear satisfied, but the crucial functional criterion – future liver remnant (FLR) volume – is missing (Analysis 2‑FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery = Missing).  
- Additional staging information that directly influences surgical planning is absent: thoraco‑CT (to rule out occult lung mets) and liver MRI (for precise lesion mapping and vascular anatomy).  
Because the adequacy of the FLR and complete extra‑hepatic staging are decisive for safe hepatectomy, the case is classified as “Potentially resectable” pending acquisition of those data (or a prerequisite intervention such as portal vein embolization if FLR proves insufficient).

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Complete pre‑operative staging  
   - Obtain thoracic CT (or PET‑CT) to confirm absence of pulmonary metastases.  
   - Perform contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with diffusion‑weighted sequences and volumetric analysis to (a) verify number/size of lesions, (b) delineate arterial/portal anatomy, (c) calculate FLR percentage.  
2. Assess need for neoadjuvant systemic therapy  
   - If FLR is adequate (> 30 % in a chemotherapy‑naïve liver) and lesions are clearly resectable, proceed directly to surgery (simultaneous or staged).  
   - If FLR is borderline (< 30 %) or if there is any uncertainty about tumor biology (CEA = 200 ng/mL, high‑risk disease), initiate conversion chemotherapy: 6 cycles of FOLFOX + cetuximab (RAS‑wild‑type) to (a) test disease biology, (b) potentially shrink lesions, and (c) allow time for FLR hypertrophy.  
3. Re‑evaluate after systemic therapy  
   - Repeat MRI and volumetry.  
   - If FLR now ≥ 30 % and all lesions remain resectable, plan definitive surgery.  
4. Surgical plan  
   - If primary tumor is asymptomatic (no obstruction, perforation or bleeding – currently Missing), perform a simultaneous sigmoid colectomy (oncologic resection with adequate lymphadenectomy) and parenchymal‑sparing liver resections (non‑anatomic wedge resections of segments II, III, V, VIII) aiming for R0 margins.  
   - If primary tumor is symptomatic or if intra‑operative assessment suggests difficulty with a combined approach, adopt a staged strategy: first resect the liver (after FLR optimization, e.g., portal vein embolization if needed), then address the sigmoid colon in a second operation.  
5. Post‑operative management  
   - Pathology review of primary and liver specimens; assess margin status and tumor regression grade.  
   - Continue adjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., additional 3–6 cycles of FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR) based on final pathology and multidisciplinary discussion.  
   - Serial CEA monitoring and imaging surveillance per standard guidelines.

Step 3 – Missing data (most crucial for the recommendation)  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) volume and functional assessment (Analysis 2‑FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery).  
- Thoraco‑CT (or PET‑CT) to definitively exclude pulmonary metastases (Analysis 2‑ThoracoCTScanPerformed = Missing).  
- Liver MRI with volumetry and vascular mapping (Analysis 2‑Has liver MRI been performed? = Missing).  
- Status of the primary colorectal tumor (has it already been resected? – Missing) and presence of obstructive, perforative or bleeding symptoms (Missing).  
- Whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been administered (Missing).  

These items must be obtained or addressed before a definitive surgical plan can be finalized.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with four peripheral liver metastases (segments II, III, V, and VIII), all smaller than 3 cm, without vascular involvement or extrahepatic disease. The distribution is bilobar but the lesions are technically amenable to multiple parenchymal-sparing resections while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number, small size, and peripheral location of metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative systemic therapy (recommended)
• The elevated CEA level (200 ng/mL) and multiplicity of lesions suggest biologically active disease.
• Given the high CEA level (200 ng/mL), perform chest CT scan and high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI).
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy according to MDT decision.
• This period treats micrometastatic disease and evaluates tumor biology.

B. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

C. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform multiple wedge/segmental resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segments II–III resections (left lateral section wedges).
– Segment V wedge resection.
– Segment VIII wedge resection.
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Management of the primary tumor
• If the sigmoid tumor has not yet been resected, a simultaneous sigmoid colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis can be considered, provided the patient’s condition allows combined surgery.
• Otherwise, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Presence of potential extra-hepatic involvement on 18FDG PET-CT and chest CT scan.
B. Detailed liver MRI describing vascular and biliary relationships of each lesion.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy.
F. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 63 years old, right-sided T4N2M1 colon cancer, two liver metastases in segments II and IVa (3 and 4 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. Liver MRI: middle hepatic vein preserved. CEA 95 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Technically resectable metastases, with priority given to controlling the primary tumor.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The liver lesions are described as “technically resectable” (2 lesions, 3 cm and 4 cm, segments II and IVa, middle hepatic vein preserved) and no extra‑hepatic disease is identified (ExtrahepaticPulmonary, Peritoneal, Lymph‑Node, Bone all Assumed False). However, a decisive technical factor – the future liver remnant (FLR) ratio – is missing (FutureLiverRemnantFLRRatio: Missing). Without confirmation that an adequate FLR (>30 % in a normal liver) can be left, the hepatic resection cannot be declared feasible. In addition, the primary tumour has not been resected (ColorectalPrimaryTumorPostResectionCharacterization: Missing) and its symptom status is unknown (obstruction, perforation, bleeding all Missing). Because these missing pieces directly impact the surgical plan, the case is classified as “Potentially resectable”.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Complete staging work‑up:

Man, 47 years old,at the abdominal CT scan T3N0 upper rectal cancer with three liver metastases (segments VI, VII and VIII), sizes 1-2 cm. CEA 60 ng/mL, RAS wild-type. No other lesions on PET.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar metastases primarily resectable, considered for combined treatment after short-course pelvic radiotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
 The three liver lesions are small (1‑2 cm) and confined to segments VI‑VIII, which can be removed with a right‑posterior sectionectomy while preserving a left‑liver remnant.  
 However, the structured analysis lacks a calculated future liver remnant (FLR) ratio and does not include a dedicated liver MRI to define arterial/portal anatomy and any vascular or biliary contact. These pieces of information are decisive for confirming that an R0 hepatic resection can be performed safely.  
 Because the MDT already plans short‑course pelvic radiotherapy before any definitive surgery, the liver resection cannot be performed “upfront” without first confirming FLR adequacy and anatomic feasibility.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Short‑course pelvic radiotherapy (SCRT) – 5 × 5 Gy for the upper‑rectal T3N0 primary (as already planned by the MDT).  
2. Neoadjuvant systemic chemotherapy – 6 cycles of a doublet regimen (e.g., FOLFOX) ± anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab) given the RAS‑wild‑type status, to:  
    assess tumor biology (“proof of time”),  
    potentially further downsize the liver metastases, and  
    treat any occult micrometastatic disease.  
3. Restaging work‑up (after chemotherapy):  
    Multiphasic liver MRI with liver‑specific contrast to delineate lesion‑vessel relationships and to calculate the FLR volume.  
    Thoraco‑CT (or chest CT) to reconfirm absence of pulmonary metastases.  
    Repeat pelvic MRI to evaluate response of the rectal tumor and to plan the definitive colorectal resection.  
4. Decision point based on restaging  
    If FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 0.4 in patients with chemotherapy‑associated liver injury) and no vascular/biliary invasion is seen, proceed to liver‑first surgery: right‑posterior sectionectomy (segments VI‑VIII) with intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm complete clearance.  
    If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy before definitive liver resection.  
5. Definitive colorectal surgery – 6–8 weeks after hepatic resection (or after PVE/second‑stage if applicable), perform total mesorectal excision (low anterior resection) with a protective loop ileostomy, guided by the post‑radiotherapy MRI response.  
6. Adjuvant systemic therapy – resume/complete peri‑operative chemotherapy (total of 12 cycles) after recovery from both surgeries, tailored to response and tolerance.  
7. Surveillance – CEA monitoring and imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 – Missing data (most crucial for the recommendation)  
 Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio – required to confirm that hepatic resection will leave sufficient functional liver.  
 Liver MRI with vascular mapping – needed to rule out hepatic artery, portal vein, or biliary involvement of the metastases and to refine the surgical plan.  
 Thoraco‑CT scan – to definitively exclude pulmonary metastases that were not documented.  
 Status of primary tumor resection – whether the rectal cancer has already been removed influences sequencing (simultaneous vs. staged).  
 Details of any prior systemic therapy – to know if the patient has already received chemotherapy and to avoid cumulative toxicity.  
 Presence of vascular or biliary contact/invasion – would alter the extent of liver resection or necessitate vascular reconstruction.  

These missing items should be obtained before finalizing the operative plan.

Case_Content:
Woman, 70 years old, history of hypertension, discovery of left colon cancer and a single 2.7 cm liver metastasis in segment IVb at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 40 ng/mL. BRAF wild-type, MSS.
MDT Discussion: Isolated metastasis, anatomically favorable for a single resection.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
• Classification: Resectable upfront  
• Reasoning: The patient has a single 2.7 cm metastasis confined to segment IVb, no extra‑hepatic disease on CT, and the lesion is anatomically favorable for a limited liver resection (segmentectomy or left lateral resection). A limited hepatic resection preserves sufficient future liver remnant in the vast majority of patients, and the primary tumour is located in the left colon, which can be safely removed in the same operation when the liver resection is minor. No vascular or biliary invasion is reported, and the size is <3 cm, meeting criteria for upfront resection as described in the literature (general principles of liver resection, technical feasibility, and adequate FLR).  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Pre‑operative MDT confirmation – verify patient’s performance status, cardiopulmonary fitness, and control of comorbidities (hypertension).  
2. Imaging confirmation – if not already performed, obtain a liver‑specific MRI (or contrast‑enhanced CT) to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement and to calculate the future liver remnant (FLR) volume.  
3. Surgical plan –  
   a. Perform a left‑sided colectomy (standard oncologic resection with adequate lymphadenectomy) for the primary tumour.  
   b. Perform a limited hepatic resection of segment IVb (segmentectomy or non‑anatomical wedge) aiming for R0 margins (>1 cm when feasible).  
   c. The combined (simultaneous) approach is appropriate because the liver resection is minor (<3 segments) and there are no obstructive or perforation symptoms from the primary tumour.  
4. Pathology review – obtain tumour grade, lymphovascular invasion, and margin status.  
5. Adjuvant systemic therapy – given synchronous disease and favourable biology (BRAF‑wt, MSS), prescribe peri‑operative chemotherapy (e.g., 6 months of FOLFOX ± biologic) after recovery from surgery, unless pathology shows low‑risk features that would allow observation.  
6. Surveillance – serial CEA measurements and cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 – Missing data (most crucial for final decision)  
- Primary tumour resection status (has the colon cancer already been removed?).  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio – needed to confirm that the remaining liver volume will be adequate after segment IVb resection.  
- Grade of differentiation of the primary tumour – influences risk of recurrence and need for adjuvant therapy.  
- Presence of vascular or biliary involvement of the liver lesion – currently missing; MRI would clarify.  
- Systemic therapy already given – unknown whether neoadjuvant chemotherapy has been administered, which could affect timing.  
- Symptoms of obstruction, perforation, or bleeding from the primary – would dictate a colon‑first approach if present.  

These items should be clarified before proceeding, but based on the available information the case is classified as resectable upfront with a simultaneous colon‑liver operation.

Potentially resectable – The MDT considers the three left‑lobe lesions technically resectable, but decisive information is missing: (a) quantitative future liver remnant (FLR) volume/ratio, (b) detailed vascular and biliary anatomy of the lesions (no liver MRI performed), and (c) whether the primary sigmoid tumour has already been resected or requires urgent surgery for obstruction/perforation. These gaps must be resolved before a definitive surgical plan can be made, therefore the case is classified as “Potentially resectable”.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• 1. Complete staging work‑up  
   – Obtain a contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with volumetry to define FLR, portal/hepatic arterial anatomy, and any vascular or biliary involvement of the metastases.  
   – Confirm the status of the primary tumour (resected vs. pending) and assess for obstructive or bleeding symptoms.  
• 2. Systemic therapy (conversion/biological)  
   – Because the tumour is KRAS‑mutated, initiate oxaliplatin‑based doublet chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX) combined with an anti‑VEGF agent (bevacizumab).  
   – Deliver 2–3 cycles (≈6–8 weeks) and restage with repeat MRI to evaluate tumour response and FLR.

   – If FLR ≥ 30 % of total liver volume and no major vascular/biliary invasion, proceed to curative surgery.

Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – the single 1.5 cm lesion in segment II is technically amenable to R0 resection, but curative surgery cannot be performed immediately because (a) the high rectal T3N1 primary requires neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (or total‑neoadjuvant therapy) before any definitive colorectal resection, and (b) definitive staging of extra‑hepatic disease (thoracic imaging) and precise hepatic anatomy (liver MRI, FLR calculation) are still missing. Until these prerequisite actions/information are obtained, the case remains “potentially resectable.”

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Initiate neoadjuvant treatment for the rectal primary: long‑course chemoradiotherapy (45‑50 Gy with concurrent 5‑FU/Capecitabine) or short‑course RT followed by consolidation chemotherapy (TNT) as recommended for T3N1 disease.  
- Concurrently start systemic chemotherapy directed at the liver metastasis (e.g., 6 cycles of FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR antibody given RAS‑wild‑type) to treat micrometastatic disease and provide a “biologic test of time.”  
- Restage after neoadjuvant therapy:  
   • Pelvic MRI to assess tumor response and circumferential margin.  
   • Multiphasic liver MRI (or contrast‑enhanced CT) to confirm size, vascular proximity, and to calculate future liver remnant (FLR) volume; aim for FLR ≥ 30 % (≥ 40 % if steatosis).  
   • Thoraco‑CT (or chest CT) to rule out pulmonary metastases.  
- If restaging shows: (i) persistent resectable liver lesion, (ii) no extra‑hepatic disease, and (iii) adequate FLR, proceed to a combined curative operation:

- Confirmation of whether the primary rectal tumor has already been resected (currently missing).  
- Timing of the liver metastasis (synchronous vs metachronous) which influences the sequencing of therapy.

- Thoraco‑CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude pulmonary metastases.

- Future liver remnant (FLR) volume/ratio.  
- Status of the primary colon tumor (resected vs. pending; presence of obstruction, perforation or bleeding).  
- Confirmation of systemic therapy already given (currently missing).  
These items must be obtained before a definitive surgical plan can be finalized.

Case_Content:
Woman, 60 years old, T3N1M1 sigmoid tumor, four bilobar liver metastases (segments II, III, VI, VIII) with one in contact with the right hepatic vein at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 240 ng/mL. RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar involvement for conversion, imaging to be re-evaluated after 4 cycles of chemotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: the current bilobar distribution (segments II, III, VI, VIII) with vascular contact (right hepatic vein) and the absence of a quantified future liver remnant (FLR) make upfront surgery unsafe. The MDT already plans a “conversion” approach after 4 cycles of chemotherapy, which is a specific prerequisite before resection can be contemplated.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate conversion systemic therapy now: oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX) combined with an anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab) because the tumor is RAS wild‑type. Plan 4–6 cycles, monitoring CEA trend.  
- At the end of chemotherapy, obtain a high‑resolution liver MRI (including hepatobiliary‑specific contrast) and repeat volumetric CT to:  
  • Measure the maximum diameter of each metastasis (to decide between wedge resection vs. anatomic resection).  
  • Define arterial, portal, and hepatic venous anatomy, especially the extent of right hepatic vein involvement.  
  • Calculate the FLR ratio; aim for ≥30 % in a normal liver (≥40 % if steatosis is present).  
- If FLR is adequate and disease has responded (no new lesions, ≤3 % growth of existing lesions), proceed to a liver‑first surgical plan:  
  • Stage 1: limited resection/ablation of the left‑lateral lesions (segments II‑III) to clear that side and preserve it as the future remnant.  
  • Perform right portal vein embolization (or ligation) to induce hypertrophy of the left liver.  
  • Allow 4–6 weeks for hypertrophy; repeat volumetry to confirm FLR adequacy.  
  • Stage 2: right‑sided hepatectomy (segments VI‑VIII) with or without vascular reconstruction of the right hepatic vein, depending on residual contact after chemotherapy.  
- After hepatic surgery, address the primary sigmoid tumor. Because there are no obstructive or bleeding symptoms, a delayed (post‑hepatectomy) laparoscopic sigmoidectomy is reasonable; simultaneous resection could be considered only if the liver operation is limited to wedge resections and operative time remains acceptable.  
- Complete a total of 6 months of peri‑operative chemotherapy (including any postoperative cycles) to treat micrometastatic disease.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
The most critical missing items that must be obtained before a definitive surgical plan can be made are:  
- Maximum (and minimum) lesion diameters of each liver metastasis.  
- Precise FLR ratio (volumetric assessment).  
- Liver MRI with detailed arterial, portal and venous anatomy.  
- Status of the primary colorectal tumor (has it been resected? any obstructive/bleeding symptoms?).  
- Histologic grade of differentiation of the primary tumor.  
These pieces of information directly influence the feasibility of a curative resection, the need for portal vein embolization or a two‑stage approach, and the sequencing of colorectal versus hepatic surgery.

Case_Content:
Man, 63 years old, left T4N2M1 colon cancer, multiple liver metastases (≥8 lesions), maximum size 4.5 cm, partial contact with the IVC at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 890 ng/mL. BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Extensive liver disease, potentially resectable after major response to FOLFOXIRI.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- The patient has ≥8 liver lesions, the largest 4.5 cm, with partial IVC contact, which makes an upfront R0 resection technically demanding.  
- Systemic therapy (FOLFOXIRI) has already been started, and the MDT notes that the disease may become resectable after a major response, indicating that a prerequisite down‑staging step is required.  
- Critical information needed to confirm feasibility (future liver remnant volume, exact segmental distribution, and presence/absence of extra‑hepatic disease) is currently missing; therefore surgery cannot be performed immediately.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Continue/optimise neoadjuvant systemic therapy  
   - Maintain FOLFOXIRI (or FOLFOXIRI + biologic) for additional cycles until maximal radiologic response is documented (RECIST criteria).  
2. Restaging work‑up  
   - Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast to delineate all lesions, vascular involvement, and segmental distribution.  
   - Obtain a thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude pulmonary, bone, or brain metastases.  
   - Re‑measure CEA; a significant decline supports favorable tumour biology.  
3. Functional liver assessment  
   - Calculate standardized future liver remnant (FLR) volume; if FLR < 30 % of total liver volume, plan portal vein embolisation (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy.  
4. Primary tumour management  
   - If the colon primary has not yet been resected and is asymptomatic, adopt a “liver‑first” strategy: resect liver disease after down‑staging, then perform definitive left‑sided colectomy.  
   - If the primary is symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding) or high‑risk, consider simultaneous resection after confirming adequate hepatic reserve.  
5. Surgical plan after down‑staging  
   - Aim for parenchymal‑sparing, margin‑negative (R0) resection of all viable metastases; consider staged hepatectomy (two‑stage or PVE‑assisted) if disease remains bilobar or FLR is marginal.  
   - Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion clearance and vascular anatomy.  
6. Post‑operative adjuvant therapy  
   - Resume systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± anti‑VEGF/EGFR based on KRAS/BRAF status) for 3–6 months after recovery, given the high tumour burden and T4N2 stage.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio and volumetric assessment.  
- Detailed hepatic segment involvement and arterial/portal anatomy.  
- Radiologic response of liver metastases to current chemotherapy (size change, number of lesions disappearing).  
- Results of thoraco‑CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic disease.  
- Status of the primary colorectal tumour (resected vs. unresected, presence of obstruction, perforation, or bleeding).  
- Histologic grade of differentiation of the primary tumour.  
These items are essential to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.

Case_Content:
Woman, 52 years old, T3N2 upper rectal adenocarcinoma with bilobar liver metastases (six lesions, 2-5 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 600 ng/mL, KRAS mutated. Liver MRI: invasion of the middle hepatic vein.
MDT Discussion: Not initially resectable, goal of volumetric reduction with chemotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
- The MDT already judged the disease “not initially resectable” because of bilobar involvement, six lesions (2‑5 cm) and invasion of the middle hepatic vein (vascular contact = True).  
- Conversion systemic chemotherapy (and subsequent volumetric assessment) is required before any curative‑intent surgery can be planned, satisfying criterion (a) for “Potentially resectable”.  
- Additional decisive information is missing (FLR ratio, hepatic segments involved, primary‑tumor resection status), but the need for neoadjuvant therapy is explicit, so the case is not classified as “Resectable upfront” nor “Not resectable”.

Step 2 - Oncological and surgical sequence  
- Conversion chemotherapy: initiate an effective doublet or triplet regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab) for at least 4 cycles (≈2 months), then restage. KRAS mutation precludes anti‑EGFR agents.  
- Restaging (CT + MRI) after 4–6 cycles to assess:  
  • Tumor response of liver lesions (size reduction, disappearance of vascular invasion).  
  • Future liver remnant (FLR) volume; calculate FLR% (target ≥ 30 % in a normal liver, ≥ 40 % after chemotherapy).  
  • Any new extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, bone, brain).  
- If FLR adequate and lesions become resectable:  
  • Liver‑first approach – proceed to hepatic surgery before the rectal primary.  
  • Technical options based on post‑chemotherapy anatomy:  
    – Parenchymal‑sparing non‑anatomic resections with R1 vascular resection of the middle hepatic vein if residual contact is limited (acceptable in KRAS‑mutated disease).  
    – If FLR would be insufficient, perform portal vein embolisation (PVE) or liver venous deprivation (LVD) to hypertrophy the remnant, then complete resection (two‑stage hepatectomy or ALPPS if rapid hypertrophy needed).  
- After hepatic clearance:  
  • Re‑evaluate the rectal primary. Upper rectal T3N2 without obstructive symptoms can be managed with total mesorectal excision (TME) after a short interval (4–6 weeks) from liver surgery. No radiotherapy is mandatory for upper rectal tumors; proceed to curative resection (low anterior resection) or consider a “liver‑first” simultaneous approach only if patient fitness permits.  
- Adjuvant therapy: complete peri‑operative systemic chemotherapy (total 6 months) – continue the same regimen post‑operatively to address micrometastatic disease.  
- Surveillance: CEA monitoring, 6‑monthly CT/MRI for the first 2 years, then annually.

Step 3 - Missing data most critical for final planning  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio – required to decide between one‑stage resection, PVE/LVD, or two‑stage/ALPPS strategy.  
- Exact hepatic segments involved – needed to map resection planes, estimate the volume of liver that will be removed, and plan vascular reconstruction if needed.  
- Status of the primary colorectal tumor (resected vs not) – influences timing (simultaneous vs liver‑first) and whether neoadjuvant radiotherapy is indicated.  
- Timing of liver metastases (synchronous vs metachronous) – impacts the aggressiveness of the conversion approach and the choice of “liver‑first” versus “classical” sequencing.  
- Arterial and biliary anatomy, presence of biliary involvement – essential for safe vascular control and to anticipate need for reconstruction.  
- Whether any systemic therapy has already been administered – determines the number of additional cycles needed and helps assess tumor biology (“proof of time”).  

Obtaining these missing pieces will allow definitive conversion to resectability and selection of the optimal surgical strategy.

The bilobar distribution, tumor burden, and venous invasion make a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant not feasible with an upfront surgical approach. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy.

A. Preoperative staging
• Given the high CEA level (600 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Conversion systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Initiate intensive doublet or triplet chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) as discussed in MDT.
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• The objective is tumor downsizing, reduction of bilobar tumor burden, and potential clearance from the middle hepatic vein.

C. Early radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT-scan every 2 months to assess:
– Response of lesions.
– Evolution of the relationship with the middle hepatic vein.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment response.

• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:
– Significant reduction in lesion size and number.
– Separation from the middle hepatic vein.
– Feasibility of staged or parenchymal-sparing resections with adequate future liver remnant.

• Two-stage hepatectomy or combined parenchymal-sparing resections depending on response pattern.
• Portal vein embolization / venous deprivation / ALPPS may be required if major hepatectomy becomes necessary.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

F. Management of the rectal primary
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles.
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles).
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. If insufficient response
• Continue systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.

Case_Content:
Man, 67 years old, T3N1M1 right colon tumor, five liver metastases (segments IV, V, VII, VIII), sizes 1.5-3.8 cm at the abdominal CT scan, CEA 270 ng/mL, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Potentially resectable after partial response to systemic therapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
 The patient has five liver metastases (segments IV, V, VII, VIII) that have shown a partial radiologic response after systemic therapy, suggesting that a curative‑intent liver resection could become feasible.  
 However, decisive information required to confirm technical resectability is missing:  
  – Thoraco‑abdominal imaging to exclude pulmonary (and other extra‑hepatic) disease (ThoracoCTScanPerformed = Missing).  
  – High‑resolution liver MRI to define lesion‑vascular relationships, biliary involvement, and to calculate the future liver remnant (FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery = Missing).  
 Because these pieces of information are essential for determining whether an R0 resection can be achieved while preserving adequate inflow, outflow, biliary drainage and sufficient FLR, the case must be classified as “Potentially resectable” pending completion of those assessments (fulfills condition b).

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Complete staging  
    Obtain a contrast‑enhanced thoracic CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out lung metastases.  
    Perform a liver‑specific MRI with diffusion‑weighted sequences to delineate tumor size, number, vascular/biliary contact, and to calculate FLR.  
2. Assess primary tumor  
    Clarify whether the right‑colon primary has been resected; if not, evaluate for symptoms of obstruction, perforation or bleeding.  
    If the primary is still in situ and asymptomatic, plan a right hemicolectomy either simultaneous with liver surgery or in a staged “liver‑first” approach, depending on operative risk and FLR.  
3. Systemic therapy  
    Continue the current chemotherapy regimen (e.g., FOLFOX ± biologic) for another 2–3 months to maximize tumor shrinkage and to serve as a biological test of disease stability.  
    Re‑image after this interval to confirm continued partial response and absence of new lesions.  
4. Functional liver reserve  
    Using the MRI‑derived volumetry, determine the FLR.  
    If FLR < 30 % (or < 20 % in patients with compromised liver), schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) or consider a two‑stage hepatectomy to induce hypertrophy before definitive resection.  
5. Surgical plan  
    Goal: R0 resection of all hepatic disease with preservation of at least two contiguous liver segments and adequate inflow/outflow.  
    Likely operation: extended right hepatectomy (segments V‑VIII) plus segment IV resection, which is a major hepatectomy (≥ 4 segments).  
    If FLR is adequate after PVE (or spontaneously), proceed to a single‑stage liver resection combined with right‑colon resection (simultaneous) or perform liver‑first resection followed by colon surgery after recovery, based on patient fitness and intra‑operative considerations.  
6. Post‑operative management  
    Pathology review for margin status and RAS‑wild‑type confirmation.  
    Resume/adapt adjuvant systemic therapy (e.g., 6 months of oxaliplatin‑based regimen) after recovery, given the high baseline CEA (270 ng/mL) and the initial stage T3 N1 M1.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
 Thoracic imaging (CT or PET‑CT) to exclude pulmonary metastases – essential to confirm that extra‑hepatic disease is absent or resectable.  
 Liver MRI with volumetric analysis – required for precise lesion mapping, assessment of vascular/biliary involvement, and calculation of the future liver remnant.  
 Current status of the primary colorectal tumor (resected vs. unresected, presence of obstructive or perforation symptoms).  
 Quantitative FLR ratio – determines need for PVE or staged hepatectomy.  
 Details on vascular contact or biliary invasion – influence technical feasibility of an R0 liver resection.

Potentially resectable: the case is deemed unresectable at presentation (bilobar disease, nine lesions, vascular contact, likely insufficient future liver remnant). Conversion therapy (systemic chemotherapy ± liver‑directed hypertrophy procedures) and additional anatomic information are required before a curative resection can be planned.

- Initiate conversion systemic chemotherapy. Because the tumour is KRAS‑mutated, use an oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX) combined with bevacizumab; give at least 4 cycles (≈2 months) and reassess with CT/MRI.  
- Perform baseline assessment of future liver remnant (FLR) using volumetric CT or MRI. If FLR is <30 % of total liver volume, plan portal vein embolisation (PVE) or liver venous deprivation (LVD) after the initial chemotherapy response to induce hypertrophy.

   • Tumour shrinkage (size of each lesion, number of viable lesions)  
   • Persistence of vascular contact/invasion  
   • FLR volume adequacy

   • First stage – clearance of disease from the future liver remnant (parenchymal‑sparing resections, possible R1 vascular resection if safe)  
   • Second stage – major hepatectomy (right/extended right or left trisection) after hypertrophy, performed 4–6 weeks after the first stage.  
   • Consider ALPPS only if hypertrophy after PVE is inadequate and the patient is fit for the higher morbidity of that technique.

   • If the patient develops obstruction, bleeding or perforation, resect the primary first (or diverting stoma).  
   • If the primary is asymptomatic, defer resection until after liver clearance (sequential primary‑first or simultaneous resection can be considered once hepatic disease is controlled and FLR is safe).  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) for 6 months, provided the patient tolerates it.  
- Throughout treatment, monitor CEA trends and obtain repeat brain MRI (to rule out the missing brain metastasis) and consider molecular work‑up for BRAF and MSI status if not already done, as this may influence future systemic options.

- Quantitative FLR ratio (future liver remnant volume)  
- Exact size (maximum and minimum diameter) of each liver lesion  
- Precise hepatic segments involved and distribution of the nine metastases  
- Status of the primary tumour (already resected or still in situ) and any obstructive/bleeding symptoms  
- Histologic grade of differentiation of the primary tumour  
- Timing of liver metastases (synchronous vs metachronous)  
- Whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been administered  
- Detailed arterial and portal venous anatomy (to plan PVE/LVD and possible vascular reconstruction)  
- Results of brain imaging (to exclude occult brain metastasis).

MDT Discussion: Not initially resectable, induction therapy planned before re-evaluation.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: the current disease burden (ten bilobar lesions up to 4 cm, vascular contact with the IVC and left portal branch) makes an immediate R0 liver resection unsafe, and the primary tumor has not yet been removed. The MDT has already planned induction systemic therapy, which is a prerequisite to achieve tumor downsizing and to allow a definitive assessment of future liver remnant (FLR) and vascular anatomy. Therefore resection can only be considered after these preparatory steps and after obtaining missing critical imaging data.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 3–4 cycles of a doublet or triplet regimen such as FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab) as induction (“neoadjuvant”) therapy for the liver metastases and to treat occult micrometastatic disease.  
- During the induction period obtain a thoraco‑CT scan to exclude pulmonary metastases and a full contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (including arterial and portal phase) to clarify hepatic arterial anatomy, extent of vascular contact, and to delineate the exact hepatic segments involved.  
- Re‑evaluate after chemotherapy:  
   • Assess radiologic response of liver lesions (size reduction, loss of IVC/portal contact).  
   • Calculate FLR volume; if FLR < 30 % (or < 20 % in a normal liver) plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or consider a two‑stage hepatectomy/ALPPS to hypertrophy the remnant.  
- Decide on the sequence of resections: because the primary right‑colon tumor is asymptomatic, a liver‑first approach is preferred to avoid loss of resectability while waiting for the primary surgery.  
- Perform curative‑intent liver surgery aiming for R0 resection:  
   • Use intra‑operative ultrasound to locate all lesions.  
   • If vascular involvement persists, consider limited vascular resection/reconstruction or ablative adjuncts (RFA/SBRT) for lesions adherent to major structures.  
   • Choose a staged or single‑stage hepatectomy based on FLR and tumor distribution.  
- After hepatic clearance and recovery, proceed to definitive right‑hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection with adequate lymphadenectomy).  
- Complete postoperative systemic therapy (additional 4–6 cycles) as adjuvant treatment, tailored to response and tolerance.  
- Follow‑up with serial CEA measurements and imaging (CT chest/abdomen, MRI liver) every 3–6 months for the first two years.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio and volumetry.  
- Detailed hepatic segment involvement and arterial anatomy.  
- Results of a thoraco‑CT scan (pulmonary metastases).  
- Confirmation of primary tumor status (resected vs. still in situ).  
- Grade of differentiation of the primary tumor.  
- Timing of liver metastases (synchronous vs. metachronous).  
These items are essential to finalize the surgical plan and to confirm that a curative‑intent resection is feasible and safe.

Potentially resectable – the case cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront” because essential information required to confirm technical feasibility is missing (future liver remnant volume, vascular/biliary involvement, and complete thoraco‑abdominal staging). The MDT already expressed that conversion “depending on response to chemotherapy” may be possible, indicating that a prerequisite systemic therapy and full imaging work‑up must be completed before surgery can be planned.

- Initiate systemic conversion chemotherapy (preferred regimen: FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab, since the tumour is KRAS‑mutated and anti‑EGFR agents are contraindicated).

- Restage after 2–3 months of therapy with:  
   • Contrast‑enhanced CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis (to rule out pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic disease).  
   • Multiphasic liver MRI with diffusion‑weighted sequences and 3‑D vascular reconstruction (to define tumour‑vessel relationships, biliary involvement, and to calculate FLR).  
   • Pelvic MRI to assess tumour response and plan total mesorectal excision (TME).  
- If restaging shows:  
   • Adequate tumour shrinkage (e.g., ≥30 % RECIST response) and CEA decline, and  
   • FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 25 % in a normal liver) with clear vascular inflow/outflow,  
   then proceed to a liver‑first curative approach:  
   • If FLR is insufficient, perform portal vein embolisation (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy (TSH) with interval chemotherapy.  
   • When FLR is sufficient, perform a parenchymal‑sparing one‑stage hepatectomy (resect all five lesions with negative margins, preserving at least two contiguous segments).

   • If the rectal tumour has achieved a good response (cT3‑cN1‑ypT0‑2), proceed with TME (low anterior resection or abdominoperineal resection as dictated by sphincter involvement).  
   • If a complete clinical response is documented, discuss organ‑preserving options (local excision or watch‑and‑wait) per current rectal cancer guidelines.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (6 months total peri‑operative chemotherapy) to consolidate response and address micrometastatic disease.  
- Ongoing surveillance with serial CEA, CT/MRI of the liver and pelvis, and chest imaging every 3–6 months for the first 2 years.

- Future liver remnant (FLR) volume/ratio.  
- Full thoraco‑abdominal staging (CT chest, CT abdomen/pelvis, liver MRI) to exclude extra‑hepatic disease and to delineate vascular/biliary involvement of the metastases.  
- Status of the primary rectal tumour (has it been resected? any obstruction, bleeding, perforation?).  
- Whether any systemic therapy has already been administered and the tumour’s radiologic response to it.  
- Detailed arterial and portal venous anatomy of the liver (to plan resection, PVE or possible vascular reconstruction).  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic metastases (lung, peritoneum, nodes, bone, brain).

Man, 62 years old, operated 4 years ago for right colon adenocarcinoma (T3N1M0), no initial recurrence. Surveillance: CEA 180 ng/mL. At the thoraco-abdominal CT scan: two liver lesions segments V and VIII, 2.8 and 3.2 cm. Liver MRI confirms no other foci. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.

Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The liver disease is limited (2 lesions, 2.8 cm and 3.2 cm in segments V and VIII) and there is no radiological evidence of extra‑hepatic spread, which satisfies the technical criteria for an R0 resection. However, the structured analysis lists the Future Liver Remnant (FLR) ratio as “Missing” and also lacks information on vascular or biliary involvement of the lesions. An adequate FLR (generally ≥30 % of total liver volume in a normal liver) and confirmation that the tumors do not encroach on major vessels are decisive for proceeding directly to surgery. Because these data are absent, the case must be classified as potentially resectable pending completion of these assessments (or a pre‑operative systemic therapy trial if the biology is deemed high‑risk).

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• 1. Confirm missing pre‑operative data: obtain quantitative FLR calculation (volumetric CT or MRI), review arterial/portal venous anatomy for vascular contact, and assess baseline liver function (bilirubin, INR, platelets).  
• 2. If FLR ≥ 30 % and no major vascular involvement: proceed with a liver‑first approach – upfront anatomical or non‑anatomical resection of segments V/VIII aiming for R0 margins, followed by adjuvant systemic therapy (e.g., 6 months of FOLFOX ± bevacizumab, appropriate for KRAS‑mutated disease).  
• 3. If FLR is insufficient or vascular contact is present: initiate neoadjuvant chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) for 2–3 months to assess disease biology (“proof of time”) and potentially induce hypertrophy of the future remnant (consider portal vein embolisation if hypertrophy is needed). Re‑image after chemotherapy; if FLR becomes adequate and lesions remain resectable, proceed to surgery as in 2.  
• 4. Post‑operative surveillance: serial CEA measurements (baseline 180 ng/mL) every 1–2 months, contrast‑enhanced liver MRI every 3–6 months, and thoraco‑abdominal CT at 6‑month intervals.  
• 5. If at any point extra‑hepatic disease appears (e.g., brain metastasis – currently “Missing”), reassess candidacy for curative intent and consider systemic therapy alone or local ablative options.

Step 3 – Missing data  
The most critical missing items that must be clarified before a definitive surgical plan can be made are:  
• Future Liver Remnant (FLR) ratio – essential to ensure postoperative liver function.  
• Presence of vascular or biliary involvement of the liver lesions – determines whether a safe margin can be achieved.  
• Baseline liver function tests and performance status (e.g., ECOG/ASA) – affect operative risk.  
• Whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been administered – influences timing of surgery and choice of peri‑operative regimen.  
• Grade of differentiation and margin status of the original right‑colon resection – provide additional prognostic context but are secondary to the FLR and vascular data.

Case_Content:
Woman, 70 years old, operated for low rectal cancer 3 years ago (T3N1M0) after chemoradiotherapy. CEA 95 ng/mL. Liver MRI: lesion in segment II (2.5 cm) and micronodule segment V. RAS wild-type, MSS.
