The patient has multiple bilobar liver metastases with the appearance of two new lesions while on FOLFOX, indicating disease progression under systemic therapy. The tumor burden, bilobar distribution, and ongoing progression make a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant not feasible at this stage. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable in the current setting.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Adaptation of systemic therapy (mandatory)
• The appearance of new lesions under FOLFOX indicates resistance to the current regimen.
• A change of systemic protocol is required according to MDT decision (e.g., switch to FOLFIRI ± targeted therapy depending on molecular profile).
• The objective is to regain disease control and potentially create a future surgical window.

B. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2 months to evaluate response to the new regimen.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

C. Criteria for reconsidering surgery
• Surgical re-evaluation can be considered only if a significant radiologic response occurs, allowing parenchymal-sparing resection with adequate future liver remnant.

D. If disease remains progressive
• Continue systemic therapy and consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).
• Consider local palliative approaches if needed according to MDT.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of all liver lesions on MRI.
B. Molecular profile beyond current data to guide systemic therapy adaptation.
C. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
D. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
E. Patient’s performance status and tolerance for further systemic therapy.
F. Presence or absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging.
G. Baseline future liver remnant (FLR) estimation in case a surgical window appears
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Man, 61 years old, left colon cancer, KRAS mutated. Ten initial liver metastases. After chemotherapy: three lesions not visualized, six stable, one progressing (segment VII, 5 cm) at the abdominal CT scan.
MDT Discussion: Heterogeneous response, feasibility of selective local treatment to be discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- Current imaging shows 7 viable liver lesions (6 stable, 1 progressing 5 cm in segment VII) after chemotherapy, indicating disease is not yet amenable to an R0 hepatectomy.  
- Key information required before a definitive surgical plan is missing: (a) thoraco‑CT to exclude pulmonary metastases, (b) liver MRI (or contrast‑enhanced MRI) to define vascular/biliary involvement and precise lesion anatomy, (c) future liver remnant (FLR) volumetry to confirm that a curative resection would leave ≥30 % functional liver, and (d) status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).  
- Because these decisive data are absent and because one lesion is progressing, surgery cannot be performed upfront; conversion or staged approaches are needed after further assessment and disease control.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Complete staging  
   - Obtain thoraco‑CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out lung metastases.  
   - Perform liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to evaluate vascular contact, biliary involvement, and to calculate FLR.  
   - Measure serum CEA (baseline and trend) to aid response monitoring.  

2. Systemic therapy (conversion)  
   - Continue/adjust systemic chemotherapy appropriate for KRAS‑mutated disease (e.g., FOLFOX + bevacizumab or FOLFIRI + bevacizumab).  
   - Aim for at least 2–3 additional cycles, reassessing response after 6–8 weeks.  

3. Local control of the progressing lesion  
   - If the segment VII lesion remains >5 cm or shows progression after systemic therapy, consider percutaneous ablative therapy (RFA or microwave) or stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) as a bridge to resection.  

4. Re‑assessment  
   - Repeat contrast‑enhanced CT/MRI and thoraco‑CT after the conversion period (≈8–12 weeks).  
   - Evaluate: (i) number and size of residual liver lesions, (ii) vascular/biliary involvement, (iii) FLR adequacy.  

5. Surgical planning  
   - If FLR ≥30 % and all lesions are resectable with negative margins, proceed to curative‑intent hepatectomy (potentially a single‑stage anatomic or non‑anatomic resection).  
   - If FLR insufficient, plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy to hypertrophy the future remnant.  
   - Primary colon tumor:  
        • If not yet resected and asymptomatic, schedule simultaneous colon resection with liver surgery (if operative risk acceptable).  
        • If symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding, perforation) or if liver surgery will be extensive, perform colon resection first, then liver surgery after recovery.  

6. Post‑operative management  
   - Adjuvant chemotherapy (same regimen as pre‑operative) for 6 months if postoperative recovery permits.  
   - Continue surveillance with periodic CT/MRI and CEA every 3–4 months for the first 2 years.  

Step 3 – Missing data (most critical for decision‑making)  
- Thoraco‑CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude pulmonary metastases.  
- Liver MRI with vascular mapping and FLR volumetry.  
- Current status of the primary colon tumor (resected vs. unresected, presence of obstructive/bleeding symptoms).  
- Serum CEA level and trend.  
- Detailed assessment of vascular or biliary involvement of the segment VII lesion.  
- Confirmation of adequate future liver remnant (FLR) percentage.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had ten liver metastases. After chemotherapy, three lesions are no longer visualized, six remain stable, and one lesion in segment VII has progressed to 5 cm. This heterogeneous response, with persistent multifocal disease and one progressing focus, makes a complete R0 resection of all initial metastatic sites unlikely while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable at this stage, though selective local strategies may be considered.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Reassessment of systemic strategy
• The progressing segment VII lesion indicates partial resistance to current chemotherapy.
• Adaptation of systemic therapy should be discussed in MDT to regain global disease control.

B. Detailed restaging and mapping
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with comparison to baseline imaging to localize all initial sites, including the “disappeared” lesions.
• Assess the precise anatomy of the progressing segment VII lesion and overall tumor distribution.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

C. Consideration of selective local treatment
• If systemic control is regained, a combined strategy may be considered:
– Parenchymal-sparing resection of the progressing segment VII lesion.
– Possible ablation/resection of other accessible stable lesions.
• The objective would be cytoreduction rather than complete clearance unless all initial sites can be addressed.

D. If global control cannot be achieved
• Continue systemic therapy and consider local ablative techniques for symptomatic or dominant lesions.
• If systemic therapy achieves only partial control, consider alternative regimens (such as local ablative techniques or intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).

Step 3 – Critical missing information

Case_Content:
Woman, 59 years old, metastatic rectal adenocarcinoma with initial bilobar involvement. After 6 cycles FOLFOXIRI: complete disappearance of lesions at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA normal.
MDT Discussion: Radiological complete response, need to assess risk of occult residual disease.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – the current data indicate a radiological complete response of the liver lesions after 6 cycles of FOLFOX‑IRI, but decisive information is missing that directly determines surgical feasibility. Specifically, a liver‑specific MRI (to confirm true disappearance and exclude occult residual disease) and a definitive assessment of the rectal primary (pelvic MRI and endoscopic evaluation) are required before any operative plan can be formulated. Until these studies are obtained, a definitive “resectable upfront” or “not resectable” classification cannot be made.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Obtain high‑quality contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (including diffusion‑weighted sequences) to verify the complete radiologic response and to evaluate for any residual viable tumor or vascular involvement that may not be seen on CT.  
• Perform pelvic MRI and a thorough endoscopic examination (including biopsies if indicated) of the rectal primary to determine whether a complete clinical response has been achieved or whether residual disease remains.  
• Review molecular profile of the tumour (RAS, BRAF, MSI‑H/dMMR) once tissue is available; this will influence any further systemic or adjuvant therapy decisions.  
• If liver MRI confirms no residual disease and the rectal tumour shows a complete clinical response (cCR) on MRI and endoscopy, consider a non‑operative “watch‑and‑wait” strategy for the primary, with intensive surveillance (clinical exam, CEA, MRI/CT every 3 months for the first 2 years).  
• If any residual liver lesion is identified on MRI, plan a curative‑intent hepatic resection. Because the disease was initially bilobar, assess future liver remnant (FLR) volume; if FLR < 30 % (or < 20 % in compromised livers), consider portal vein embolisation or a two‑stage hepatectomy before definitive resection.  
• If the rectal primary remains viable, schedule a total mesorectal excision (TME) after hepatic surgery (simultaneous or staged according to patient fitness and anatomical considerations).  
• Given the complete radiologic response and normalized CEA, no additional adjuvant chemotherapy is mandatory; however, a short course of maintenance therapy (e.g., fluoropyrimidine ± biologic) may be discussed in MDT if high‑risk molecular features are present.  
• Throughout, maintain multidisciplinary follow‑up with colorectal surgery, hepatobiliary surgery, medical oncology, radiology, and pathology to reassess resectability after each step.

Step 3 – Missing data (most crucial)  
• Liver MRI (to confirm true complete response and assess vascular/biliary involvement).  
• Pelvic MRI and endoscopic assessment of the rectal primary (to determine need for primary resection versus watch‑and‑wait).  
• Status of primary tumour resection (has it already been removed or not).  
• Future liver remnant (FLR) calculation.  
• Molecular phenotype of the tumour (RAS, BRAF, MSI‑H/dMMR).  
• Brain imaging (to rule out occult cerebral metastasis).  
These items are essential to finalize resectability classification and to design a safe, curative‑intent surgical plan.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had bilobar liver metastases. After 6 cycles of FOLFOXIRI, CT shows complete radiological disappearance of all lesions and CEA has normalized. Despite this apparent complete response, the high risk of occult residual microscopic disease at the sites of the initial metastases makes the situation potentially resectable after conversion therapy, but not safely classifiable as disease-free without precise remapping of the original disease.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion-weighted sequences and compare meticulously with baseline imaging.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, even if no lesion is currently visible.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy based on the initial disease map
• If technically feasible, plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided approach targeting the original metastatic locations, not only visible lesions.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to detect occult residual disease.
• Depending on distribution, a staged approach may be required.

C. If surgical targeting of all initial sites is not feasible
• Continue systemic therapy and close imaging surveillance.
• Consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal strategy.

D. Integration with rectal primary management
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles) + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
• Coordinate pelvic treatment and timing of rectal surgery with the hepatic surgical plan according to rectal oncologic principles.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• If surgery is performed, resume systemic therapy to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial lesions on baseline imaging.
B. Precise localization of the initial metastases relative to vascular structures.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Status and management plan of the rectal primary tumor : circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI, essential for rectal surgical planning. 
E. Patient’s performance status for potential staged hepatectomy.
F. Confirmation of absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging.
G. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer with bulky metastases. After 8 cycles of chemotherapy: incomplete reduction, persistence of three lesions >5 cm. CEA 450 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Partial response insufficient, no criteria for immediate resectability.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: After 8 cycles of chemotherapy the three liver lesions remain >5 cm, indicating bulky disease that may be technically challenging. Critical anatomic information is missing (hepatic segments involved, vascular or biliary contact, arterial anatomy, future liver remnant volume) and extra‑hepatic staging has not been performed (no thoraco‑abdominal CT, no liver MRI). Without these data a definitive judgment on whether an R0 resection preserving two contiguous segments and adequate FLR can be achieved is impossible. Therefore resection cannot be offered upfront; further staging and possibly additional conversion therapy are required before a surgical plan can be finalized.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Complete staging  
   • Obtain contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary, nodal, peritoneal, bone or brain metastases.  
   • Perform liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to delineate lesion number, exact segmental distribution, vascular/biliary involvement, and to calculate standardized future liver remnant (FLR) volume.  
2. Assess the primary tumor  
   • Determine whether the right‑sided primary has been resected; if not, evaluate for symptoms (obstruction, bleeding, perforation).  
   • If the primary is still in situ and symptomatic, plan either a diverting colostomy or definitive right hemicolectomy before or concurrently with liver surgery (reverse‑sequence “liver‑first” approach is preferred when the liver disease is the limiting factor).  
3. Optimize systemic therapy  
   • Continue or modify systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or FOLFIRI plus a biologic agent) for an additional 2–3 months aiming for further tumor shrinkage, especially if imaging shows only partial response.  
   • Consider switching to a more intensive regimen (triplet chemotherapy ± anti‑EGFR/anti‑VEGF) if the disease is still progressing.  
4. Re‑assessment after conversion therapy  
   • Repeat liver MRI and CT to evaluate lesion size reduction, relationship to major vessels, and FLR.  
   • If lesions become ≤5 cm and a margin‑negative (R0) resection can be achieved while preserving ≥20–30 % FLR, proceed to curative‑intent hepatectomy.  
   • If FLR is insufficient, plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy (including possible ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy before definitive resection.  
5. Surgical approach  
   • Aim for parenchymal‑sparing, anatomic or non‑anatomic resections that leave at least two contiguous liver segments with intact inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  
   • Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm no occult lesions.  
6. Post‑operative management  
   • Resume/adapt adjuvant systemic therapy (typically 3–6 months) based on pathology and molecular profile.  
   • Consider peri‑operative liver protection strategies (avoid excessive steatosis, monitor for sinusoidal injury).  

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
• Detailed hepatic anatomy: segments involved, vascular/biliary contact, arterial anatomy, presence of portal thrombosis.  
• Quantitative FLR assessment (volume or functional measurement).  
• Full extra‑hepatic staging (thoracic CT or PET‑CT, assessment for lung, peritoneal, nodal, bone, brain disease).  
• Molecular phenotype of the primary tumor (RAS, BRAF, MSI status) and grade of differentiation – needed for prognosis and choice of biologic agents.  
• Status of the primary colorectal tumor (resected or not, presence of obstruction/bleeding/perforation).  
• Results of liver MRI (or high‑quality contrast CT) to confirm lesion characteristics and feasibility of R0 resection.  

Acquiring these missing pieces will allow a definitive decision between proceeding to curative liver surgery or continuing conversion therapy/alternative locoregional treatments.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had bulky liver metastases. After 8 cycles of chemotherapy, there is only partial reduction with persistence of three large lesions >5 cm and persistently elevated CEA (450 ng/mL). The residual tumor burden and limited response make a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant not achievable at this stage. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable in the current setting.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Adaptation of systemic therapy (mandatory)
• The insufficient response to current chemotherapy requires modification of the systemic regimen or consider intra arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary cancer, according to MDT decision.
• The objective remains to achieve further tumor downsizing that may open a future surgical window.

B. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2 months to evaluate response to the new regimen.
• Given the high CEA level (450 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to confirm absence of additional occult lesions.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

C. Criteria for reconsidering surgery
• Surgical re-evaluation can be considered only if a significant radiologic response occurs, reducing lesion size and allowing parenchymal-sparing resection with adequate future liver remnant.

D. If disease remains insufficiently responsive
• Continue systemic therapy and consider local palliative approaches if needed according to MDT.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of the residual lesions on MRI.
B. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
C. Patient’s performance status and tolerance for further systemic therapy.
D. Presence or absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging.
E. Previous systemic regimens received and tolerance.
F. Baseline future liver remnant (FLR) estimation in case a surgical window appears.
G. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Man, 63 years old, operated two years earlier with a right hepatectomy for synchronous metastases from a left colon cancer. Surveillance: CEA 220 ng/mL. Liver MRI: two lesions segments II and III (2.1 and 3.4 cm). KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Contralateral liver recurrence, anatomically accessible, no extra-hepatic disease.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: the current liver lesions are anatomically accessible, but a definitive decision cannot be made without a quantitative assessment of the future liver remnant (FLR) after planned resection of segments II and III. The structured analysis lists “FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery: Missing,” which is a decisive missing piece of information. If the FLR would be insufficient (<30 % of total liver volume or <0.5 % of body‑weight ratio), an upfront repeat hepatectomy would be unsafe and the case would shift to non‑resectable. Conversely, if volumetry shows an adequate FLR (e.g., after hypertrophy techniques), a limited resection or combined resection‑ablation could be pursued. Therefore the case is classified as potentially resectable pending FLR evaluation (and, if needed, portal vein embolisation or other hypertrophy strategies).

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Confirm status of the primary colorectal tumor – verify that the left‑colon primary has been resected with negative margins; if not, plan either (a) primary resection first (if symptomatic) or (b) simultaneous primary‑plus‑liver surgery if the liver surgery is limited.  
2. Obtain complete pre‑operative imaging –  
   • Contrast‑enhanced CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis (to rule out occult extra‑hepatic disease).  
   • Triphasic liver CT or MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast to delineate arterial anatomy, capsular infiltration and to perform volumetric analysis for FLR.  
3. Systemic chemotherapy (neoadjuvant) – because the tumour is KRAS‑mutated, use an oxaliplatin‑based doublet (e.g., mFOLFOX6) combined with bevacizumab, or a triplet (FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab) if the patient is fit. Aim for 2–3 cycles (≈6–8 weeks) to achieve disease control and possible tumour shrinkage.  
4. Re‑assessment after chemotherapy – repeat liver MRI with volumetry. If the FLR is ≥30 % (or remnant‑to‑body‑weight ratio ≥ 0.5 %) and the lesions have responded (size ≤2 cm or amenable to limited wedge resection), proceed to curative‑intent surgery:  
   • Option A: Limited anatomical resection (segment II or III) preserving as much left‑lateral parenchyma as possible, aiming for R0 margins.  
   • Option B: If complete resection would compromise FLR, perform percutaneous ablative therapy (RFA or microwave) for one or both lesions, combined with limited resection of the remaining lesion.  
5. If FLR remains inadequate after chemotherapy, consider portal vein embolisation of the right portal branch (already resected) is not feasible; therefore, the only realistic curative approach is non‑surgical local therapy (ablation, stereotactic body radiotherapy) together with continued systemic treatment.  
6. Post‑operative/adjuvant phase – continue systemic chemotherapy (total of 6 months peri‑operative therapy) and schedule regular CEA monitoring and imaging (CEA every 2 months, liver MRI/CT every 3–6 months).  

Step 3 - Missing data  
• FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery (quantitative future liver remnant volume).  
• Arterial anatomy of the left liver (to plan safe inflow/outflow preservation).  
• Presence of capsular infiltration or non‑nodular infiltrative pattern (affects resectability).  
• Status of the primary colorectal tumour resection (already resected or not).  
• Details of any prior systemic therapy (type, response).  
These missing items are the most critical for confirming whether a repeat hepatectomy can be performed safely or whether the plan must rely on non‑surgical local therapies.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with two metachronous liver metastases in segments II and III (2.1 and 3.4 cm) occurring in the left lateral section after a prior right hepatectomy, without evidence of extrahepatic disease. The lesions are peripherally located but arise in the only remaining functional liver. Resection is technically feasible but must strictly preserve adequate parenchyma and inflow/outflow. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria in the setting of previous major hepatectomy, this pattern is considered potentially resectable with a strict parenchymal-sparing strategy, pending volumetric confirmation.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory preoperative volumetric and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships and a chest CT scan.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (which is the current liver) and ensure preservation of sufficient functional parenchyma.
• Assess portal inflow and venous outflow carefully given prior right hepatectomy.

B. Peri-operative systemic therapy
• Given the elevated CEA (220 ng/mL) and early recurrence, a short course (2–3 months) of peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) may be considered.
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT-scan after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

D. Surgical management after restaging
• If resectability and adequate FLR are confirmed, perform parenchymal-sparing resections or ablation of the 2 lesions of segments II and III aiming for R0 margins.
• Avoid any formal left hepatectomy or extended resection.
• Depending on lesion distribution and FLR, this may be performed in a single stage or staged approach.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.
E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles if given.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Detailed vascular and biliary anatomy of segments II and III on MRI.
B. Exact volumetric assessment of the remaining liver (future liver remnant).
C. Grade of differentiation, MSS/ MSI mutation and molecular profile of the primary cancer: influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy.
D. Details of previous chemotherapy received before/after the first hepatectomy.
E. a chest CT scan F. Exact CEA trend prior to detection of recurrence.
G. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 70 years old, history of left R0 hepatectomy for liver metastases three years ago. CEA 180 ng/mL. Liver MRI: single lesion segment VIII (3.8 cm) in contact with the IVC. RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Deep solitary recurrence, technical assessment of resection required.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: the solitary segment VIII metastasis contacts the IVC, and the patient has already undergone a left hepatectomy, so the future liver remnant (FLR) may be limited. The structured analysis lacks a FLR ratio assessment and does not provide a complete thoraco‑abdominal staging to exclude extra‑hepatic disease. Both the FLR adequacy and the presence/absence of distant metastases are decisive for proceeding to surgery; therefore resection cannot be performed upfront and requires further evaluation (and possibly down‑staging chemotherapy or portal vein embolization) before a definitive surgical plan.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Complete restaging: obtain a contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal or bone metastases that were not reported.  
- Perform CT‑based volumetry of the liver to calculate the FLR; if the FLR is <30 % of total liver volume (or <40 % in a liver previously exposed to chemotherapy), plan a pre‑operative liver hypertrophy maneuver (portal vein embolization of the right portal branches or ALPPS) to increase the remnant.  
- Initiate systemic therapy: given RAS‑wild‑type disease and a high CEA (180 ng/mL), start a 2‑month oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX or CAPOX) with an anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab) to assess tumor biology and attempt modest downsizing of the IVC‑adjacent lesion.  
- Re‑image after chemotherapy (MRI with liver‑specific contrast) to evaluate response, reassess vascular involvement, and repeat FLR calculation.  
- If the lesion remains resectable (clear margins achievable, IVC involvement limited to contact without invasion) and the FLR is adequate, proceed to a parenchymal‑sparing segmentectomy of segment VIII with vascular control; intra‑operative ultrasound should be used to confirm margins and IVC relationship. Vascular reconstruction (patch or limited IVC resection) should be prepared if true invasion is identified.  
- Post‑operative plan: administer adjuvant chemotherapy (total 6 months of systemic therapy) given the recurrent nature of disease and elevated CEA.  
- Surveillance: CEA measurement and cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months thereafter.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Quantitative FLR ratio (future liver remnant volume) – essential to determine whether a single‑stage resection is safe.  
- Full thoraco‑abdominal imaging results (presence or absence of extra‑hepatic metastases).  
- Detailed hepatic arterial and venous anatomy around the segment VIII lesion (relationship to hepatic veins and IVC).  
- Status of the primary colorectal tumor (resected or still present, location, nodal stage).  
- Baseline liver function tests and any prior chemotherapy‑induced liver injury (steatosis, sinusoidal obstruction). These items are the most critical gaps that must be filled before a definitive surgical decision can be made.

• Perform expert liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to precisely evaluate the relationship of the lesion to the IVC and right hepatic vein and a chest CT scan.

• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT-scan after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

• If resectability is confirmed, proceed with an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resection of segment VIII.
• The goal is R0 resection while strictly preserving hepatic inflow/outflow.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles if given.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Case_Content:
Man, 59 years old, left hepatectomy performed two years prior. Liver MRI: three new lesions (segments V, VI, VII) measuring 1.5 to 2.8 cm.On the thoracic CT scan no other metastases. KRAS mutated, CEA 480 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Multiple liver recurrence, feasibility of local treatment to be re-evaluated.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Classification: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: The three recurrent liver lesions are confined to the right liver (segments V‑VI‑VII) after a previous left hepatectomy, making a curative resection technically feasible only if a sufficient future liver remnant (FLR) remains. The structured analysis lists “FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery: Missing,” which is a decisive piece of information for determining whether resection can be performed safely. Additionally, the presence or absence of vascular or biliary involvement of the lesions is not reported (“PresenceOfVascularContactOrInvasion: Missing”). Because these critical data are lacking, the case cannot be declared “Resectable upfront.” No oncological contraindication (e.g., extra‑hepatic disease) is present, so the lesions are not “Not resectable.” Therefore the appropriate category is “Potentially resectable” pending completion of the missing assessments and, likely, neoadjuvant systemic therapy to downsize disease and test tumor biology.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Baseline systemic therapy – Initiate conversion chemotherapy appropriate for KRAS‑mutated disease (e.g., mFOLFOX + bevacizumab) for 2–3 months.  
2. Imaging reassessment – After 2 cycles, repeat high‑resolution liver MRI (with hepatobiliary contrast) and CT volumetry to:  
   - Quantify FLR (target ≥ 30 % of total liver volume for chemotherapy‑injured liver).  
   - Evaluate vascular/biliary contact of the V‑VI‑VII lesions.  
   - Detect any occult extra‑hepatic disease (including lymph nodes and brain).  
3. Decision point  
   - If FLR adequate and no major vascular/biliary invasion: proceed to curative‑intent, parenchymal‑sparing resection of the involved segments (segmental or non‑anatomic resections of V, VI, VII) with intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion clearance and achieve R0 margins.  
   - If FLR insufficient: consider portal vein embolization (PVE) of the right portal branches feeding the diseased segments, followed by repeat volumetry after 4–6 weeks; if FLR then meets criteria, perform the staged hepatectomy.  
   - If lesions are close to major vessels or not amenable to safe resection: employ locoregional ablative modalities (RFA or microwave) for the individual lesions, either percutaneously or intra‑operatively, combined with limited resection of any remaining disease.  
4. Post‑operative management – Resume systemic therapy (e.g., continuation of the same regimen or switch to second‑line based on response) for 3–6 months as adjuvant treatment. Monitor CEA every 1–2 months and perform imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–6 months.  
5. Multidisciplinary review – Throughout the process, maintain MDT discussions (surgery, medical oncology, radiology, interventional radiology) to adjust the plan based on response, liver function, and patient performance status.

- Quantitative FLR volume/ratio to confirm that a safe liver remnant will remain after resection.  
- Detailed vascular and biliary anatomy of the lesions (presence of portal/hepatic vein or bile duct involvement).  
- Whether the primary colorectal tumor has already been resected and its location (right vs. left colon) – influences surveillance and potential need for additional colorectal surgery.  
- Current systemic therapy status (has the patient already received chemotherapy for this recurrence?).  
- Assessment of extra‑hepatic lymph‑node disease (imaging of abdominal nodes) and brain imaging (to rule out occult metastases).  
- Patient’s performance status and liver function tests (to gauge tolerance of chemotherapy and major surgery).

MDT Discussion: Late liver recurrence, no other locations, satisfactory liver volume.

Woman, 55 years old, history of left hepatectomy for synchronous metastases. Surveillance: CEA 560 ng/mL. Liver MRI: multiple lesions in right and left lobes (up to 4.5 cm). RAS wild-type.

Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has diffuse bilobar recurrence after a prior left hepatectomy, with lesions up to 4.5 cm in both lobes. Critical information that determines technical feasibility is missing – namely the future liver remnant (FLR) volume and its functional adequacy, the exact number and segmental distribution of lesions, and any vascular or biliary involvement. Without these data a safe curative resection cannot be confirmed. Because the disease could become resectable after down‑staging or after strategies to augment the FLR (e.g., portal vein embolisation, two‑stage hepatectomy, ALPPS), the case fits the “potentially resectable” category as defined by the need for a specific prerequisite (assessment/augmentation of FLR) before surgery.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Complete restaging  
   – Perform thoraco‑abdominal contrast‑enhanced CT (or PET‑CT) and repeat liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast to define the exact number, size, segmental location, vascular/biliary contact, and to rule out extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, nodes, bone, brain).  
   – Calculate the standardized FLR volume (CT‑volumetry) and assess liver function (ICG clearance, liver biochemistry).  
   – Verify status of the colorectal primary (resected or still in situ, symptoms).  

• Multidisciplinary review of restaging results.  

• Systemic therapy (conversion chemotherapy)  
   – Initiate a doublet regimen (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI) combined with a biologic agent appropriate for RAS‑wild‑type disease (cetuximab or panitumumab).  
   – Aim for 2–3 cycles, then re‑image to assess radiologic response (RECIST) and CEA trend.  

• If disease responds (≥30 % reduction of total tumor volume) and FLR is projected to be ≥30 % of total liver (or ≥0.5 % body‑weight ratio) after planned resection:  
   – Consider portal vein embolisation of the diseased lobe to hypertrophy the future remnant, followed by repeat imaging in 4–6 weeks.  
   – If FLR remains insufficient, plan a two‑stage hepatectomy (first stage: clear lesions from the future remnant, second stage after hypertrophy) or, in selected centres with expertise, ALPPS.  
   – Aim for parenchymal‑sparing resections with negative margins (R0/R1 acceptable if <1 mm).  

• If extra‑hepatic metastases are identified and are limited (oligometastatic) and resectable, incorporate simultaneous or staged extra‑hepatic resections into the plan.  

• If there is no adequate response, FLR remains inadequate, or extra‑hepatic disease is extensive, continue systemic therapy with best‑available regimen and consider liver‑directed palliative options (radiofrequency/microwave ablation, selective internal radiation therapy, or trans‑arterial chemo‑embolisation) rather than curative surgery.  

• After any curative‑intent liver resection, resume adjuvant systemic therapy (typically 6 months) and maintain surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3–6 months.

Step 3 – Missing data  
The most decisive missing items that must be obtained before a definitive surgical plan can be made are:  
- Precise future liver remnant (FLR) volume and functional assessment.  
- Exact number of hepatic metastases, their segmental distribution, and any vascular or biliary invasion.  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, nodal, bone, brain).  
- Status of the colorectal primary (resected or still present, symptomatic).  
- Whether the patient has already received systemic chemotherapy and her response to it.  

These data will determine whether the patient can be down‑staged to a resectable state and which hepatic‑preserving strategy (PVE, two‑stage hepatectomy, ALPPS) is appropriate.

Therefore the appropriate category is “Potentially resectable”, pending clarification of vascular/biliary involvement (or completion of a short course of down‑staging chemotherapy that would also serve as biologic selection).

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Step 2.1 Imaging clarification – Perform a high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast (or contrast‑enhanced CT angiography) to define the proximity of the IVb and II lesions to the hepatic veins, portal branches and biliary ducts.  
- Step 2.2 Systemic therapy (down‑staging / biologic selection) – Because the disease is metachronous, CEA is markedly elevated (300 ng/mL) and the known KRAS mutation predicts lack of benefit from anti‑EGFR antibodies, initiate 2–3 months of oxaliplatin‑based doublet chemotherapy (mFOLFOX6) combined with bevacizumab. This regimen has shown conversion and R0 rates of ~30‑40 % in KRAS‑mutated CRLM and can lower tumor burden while providing a “proof of time”.  
- Step 2.3 Restaging – Repeat liver MRI (and thoraco‑abdominal CT) after chemotherapy. Confirm that the lesions are still limited to segments IVb and II, that there is no new extra‑hepatic disease (brain imaging if clinically indicated), and that vascular/biliary involvement remains absent.  
- Step 2.4 Surgical plan – If restaging shows stable or responding disease and clear margins are feasible, schedule a parenchyma‑sparing left‑lateral/segmental resection (segment II ± IVb) or combined resection + intra‑operative ablation for any lesion abutting critical structures. Ensure a minimum of 4–6 weeks interval after the last bevacizumab dose to reduce bleeding risk.  
- Step 2.5 Post‑operative management – Resume the same systemic regimen (or an appropriate adjuvant protocol) for 6 months post‑resection, given the high CEA and KRAS‑mutated biology.  
- Step 2.6 Surveillance – Monitor CEA every 1–2 months and perform cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then at increasing intervals, to detect early recurrence.

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Presence of vascular contact or invasion (critical for confirming R0 feasibility).  
- Presence of biliary structure involvement.  
- Detailed status of the colorectal primary (location, grade, whether it has been resected).  
- Confirmation that there is no brain metastasis (ExtrahepaticBrainInvolvement is Missing).  
- Patient’s performance status, comorbidities and baseline liver function (to ensure tolerance of chemotherapy and surgery).  
These missing items are the most pivotal for finalizing the resectability decision and tailoring the peri‑operative oncologic plan.

Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Classification: Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has two small liver metastases confined to segments II and III (2.4 cm and a micronodule) after a previous segmental VI‑VII resection. Technically a left‑lateral (segments II‑III) resection would be feasible, but the adequacy of the future liver remnant (FLR) is unknown – the structured analysis lists “FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery: Missing.” Because the remaining liver volume after removing the left‑lateral sector may be borderline given the prior right‑posterior resection, a definitive decision requires quantitative FLR assessment (or, if insufficient, portal vein embolisation or a two‑stage approach). Therefore the case meets the definition of “Potentially resectable” (a specific prerequisite – FLR evaluation – is needed before surgery).

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Complete staging  
   • Obtain a contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out extra‑hepatic disease (the analysis shows thoraco‑CT not performed).  
   • Repeat liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast if needed for precise volumetry.  
   • Measure serum CEA and assess performance status, liver function, and comorbidities.  

2. Future liver remnant assessment  
   • Perform volumetric CT or MRI to calculate FLR as a percentage of total liver volume.  
   • If FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % in a patient with prior chemotherapy), proceed to surgery.  
   • If FLR < 30 %, plan portal vein embolisation (PVE) of the right portal branches to hypertrophy the left‑medial and right‑anterior segments, with repeat volumetry after 4–6 weeks.  

3. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (optional)  
   • Because the disease is metachronous and limited, peri‑operative (neoadjuvant) chemotherapy is not mandatory but may be considered to obtain “proof of time” and treat occult micrometastases, especially if FLR is marginal. A standard oxaliplatin‑based doublet (e.g., CAPOX) for 2–3 cycles can be used.  

4. Surgical resection  
   • If FLR is adequate, schedule a minimally invasive (laparoscopic or robotic) left‑lateral sectionectomy (segments II‑III) with intra‑operative ultrasound to locate the micronodule in segment II and ensure negative margins (R0).  
   • Preserve at least two contiguous segments with intact inflow/outflow and biliary drainage, as recommended in the literature.  

5. Post‑operative management  
   • Resume or initiate adjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., 6 months of CAPOX) to address micrometastatic disease, given the metachronous nature.  
   • Follow‑up with serial CEA, CT chest/abdomen every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 – Missing data (most crucial for decision‑making)  
- Quantitative FLR ratio (future liver remnant volume).  
- Thoraco‑CT (or equivalent) to exclude pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic metastases.  
- Confirmation that the primary colorectal tumor has already been resected and its pathology (margin status, T/N stage).  
- Current CEA level and any symptoms from the primary site (obstruction, bleeding, perforation).  
- Details of any prior systemic therapy and its response.  
- Vascular or biliary involvement of the new lesions (vascular contact, portal/hepatic vein proximity).  

These missing items should be obtained promptly to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.

Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: the solitary 3.1 cm recurrence in segment VIII is technically amenable to a limited resection, but decisive information is missing. The future liver remnant (FLR) volume after a repeat right‑sided resection has not been quantified, and no cross‑sectional staging (chest/abdomen CT) has been documented to exclude extra‑hepatic disease. Because FLR adequacy and the presence/absence of distant metastases are essential to determine whether a curative hepatectomy can be performed safely, the case must be classified as “Potentially resectable” pending these data.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Complete restaging: obtain a contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal or osseous metastases; repeat high‑quality liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast for precise volumetry and vascular mapping (arterial, portal, hepatic veins).  
• Assess liver function (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count) and calculate FLR ratio using CT volumetry; target FLR ≥ 30 % for a liver previously exposed to chemotherapy (or ≥ 20 % if liver parenchyma is pristine).  
• If FLR is insufficient, consider pre‑operative strategies (e.g., right portal vein embolization – although left lobe is already resected, the remaining right‑lateral segments can be hypertrophied, or an ALPPS‑type approach if feasible) or alternatively local ablative therapy (RFA/MWA) as a bridge.  
• Initiate systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 2–3 cycles of FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) to treat occult micrometastatic disease and to assess tumor biology; monitor CEA trend (baseline 200 ng/mL).

• Post‑operative management: resume adjuvant systemic therapy (completion of a standard 6‑month peri‑operative regimen) and schedule regular CEA and imaging surveillance (every 3–4 months for the first 2 years).  

Step 3 – Missing data  
• Future liver remnant volume/FLR ratio (critical for safety of repeat resection).  
• Comprehensive thoraco‑abdominal staging (CT or PET‑CT) to exclude extra‑hepatic metastases.  
• Detailed hepatic arterial and portal venous anatomy, and relationship of the tumor to the middle hepatic vein (to plan vein preservation or reconstruction).  
• Status of prior systemic therapy and timing of recurrence (metachronous vs synchronous).  
• Baseline liver function tests and assessment of chemotherapy‑induced liver injury (steatosis, sinusoidal obstruction).  
These missing items are the most pivotal for confirming resectability and finalizing the treatment plan.

Response:

Resectable upfront  

Reasoning: The patient has a solitary 3.9 cm metastasis confined to segment VII, no extra‑hepatic disease on CT, and the lesion is anatomically approachable according to the MDT. Prior bisegmentectomy of IV‑V leaves the right posterior sector (VI‑VII‑VIII) and the left liver available; a segmentectomy of VII would preserve at least two contiguous segments (e.g., VI and VIII) with adequate inflow/outflow and is expected to leave >30 % future liver remnant in a non‑cirrhotic liver. No vascular or biliary invasion is reported. Therefore, curative resection can be performed immediately without mandatory pre‑operative down‑staging.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Pre‑operative work‑up  
   • Verify performance status, liver function tests, and obtain a recent CEA level (missing in the analysis).  
   • Review cross‑sectional imaging (CT/MRI) with a hepatobiliary radiologist; perform intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion size, location and rule out occult additional disease.  
   • Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR) volume; if <30 % (or <40 % after prior chemotherapy) consider portal vein embolisation (PVE) or a two‑stage approach – but this is unlikely given the limited resection required.  

2. Surgical treatment (first definitive step)  
   • Anatomical segmentectomy of segment VII (or non‑anatomical wedge resection with ≥1 cm margin) aiming for R0 resection.  
   • Preserve at least two contiguous segments with intact inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  
   • Use intra‑operative ultrasound to detect any additional sub‑centimetric lesions; treat them with ablation if present and resectable.  

3. Post‑operative systemic therapy  
   • Because the tumour is KRAS‑mutated (RAS‑mut), adjuvant chemotherapy with an oxaliplatin‑based regimen (e.g., mFOLFOX6) plus bevacizumab is appropriate, following the protocol used in the cited prospective study where KRAS‑mut patients received bevacizumab.  
   • Start adjuvant therapy within 6–8 weeks after surgery, once wound healing is adequate.  

4. Surveillance  
   • CEA measurement every 1–2 months for the first 6 months, then every 3–6 months.  
   • Contrast‑enhanced liver MRI or CT every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually, to detect recurrence early.  

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
• Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio – needed to confirm that resection will leave sufficient functional liver.  
• Primary tumour status (has the colorectal primary already been resected? location, stage, margin status) – influences need for additional colorectal surgery or adjuvant therapy.  
• CEA level – baseline tumour marker for postoperative surveillance and to help assess disease activity.  
• Timing of the liver metastasis (synchronous vs metachronous) – informs prognosis and the urgency of systemic therapy.  
• Details on vascular or biliary involvement of the segment VII lesion – could alter the extent of resection or require vascular reconstruction.  

These missing items should be obtained before proceeding, but none of them currently preclude an upfront curative liver resection.

    Repeat liver MRI (or contrast‑enhanced CT) and repeat CEA measurement.

Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
• Classification: Potentially resectable  
• Reasoning: The case lacks decisive anatomic information required to confirm that an R0 hepatic resection can be achieved (hepatic segments involved, vascular contact/invasion, arterial anatomy, FLR ratio) and it is unknown whether the bilateral pulmonary nodules are surgically resectable or represent benign lesions. Because these missing data directly determine technical feasibility, the patient cannot be offered an upfront operation and must first undergo further staging and/or down‑staging therapy before a definitive surgical plan can be made.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Baseline staging completion  
   – Obtain a contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (including gadoxetic‑acid sequences) to delineate segmental involvement, vascular relationships and to calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).  
   – Perform a PET‑CT (or at minimum a high‑resolution chest CT with measurement of pulmonary nodules) to confirm metastatic nature of the lung lesions, assess size, relationship to bronchi/vessels and to detect any additional extra‑hepatic disease.  
2. Systemic induction therapy  
   – Start a standard first‑line doublet or triplet regimen for KRAS‑mutated disease (e.g., FOLFOX or FOLFIRI + bevacizumab) for 4–6 cycles.  
   – Re‑assess tumor markers (CEA) after chemotherapy; a falling CEA supports response.  
3. Re‑evaluation after chemotherapy  
   – Repeat liver MRI and chest imaging to determine:  
        • Whether the three liver lesions have downsized or become more amenable to resection (e.g., conversion to ≤4 cm, clear margins, no major vascular encasement).  
        • Whether the FLR is adequate; if not, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or ALPPS to induce hypertrophy before hepatectomy.  
        • Whether the pulmonary nodules are resectable (≤5 cm, limited number, adequate pulmonary reserve).  
4. Surgical sequencing (reverse/liver‑first approach) – Assuming:  
   – The primary left‑sided colon tumour is asymptomatic (no obstruction, perforation or bleeding reported).  
   – Liver disease is resectable after induction therapy and FLR is sufficient.  
   Then:  
        a. Perform hepatic resection (preferably parenchyma‑sparing; major or minor hepatectomy according to segmental distribution).  
        b. After hepatic recovery (≈6–8 weeks), address the colorectal primary (segmental colectomy) if it has not yet been removed.  
        c. If pulmonary metastases are deemed resectable and the patient’s pulmonary function is adequate, schedule staged thoracic metastasectomy (typically after primary colon resection) or consider simultaneous liver‑lung resection only in highly selected centres with expertise.  
5. If liver or lung disease remains unresectable after chemotherapy – Continue systemic therapy, consider local ablative modalities (RFA/MWA, stereotactic body radiotherapy) for residual liver lesions, and/or stereotactic lung radiotherapy for pulmonary nodules.  

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
• Liver MRI with detailed segmental and vascular anatomy (to define resectability and calculate FLR).  
• Quantified future liver remnant ratio (to decide need for PVE or staged hepatectomy).  
• Precise size, location and resectability assessment of the bilateral pulmonary nodules (including PET confirmation).  
• Status of the primary colon tumour (already resected or still in situ; presence of obstruction, perforation or bleeding).  
• Histologic grade of differentiation of the primary tumour (prognostic and may influence aggressiveness of the treatment plan).
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with three liver metastases (2–4 cm) and two bilateral pulmonary nodules in the setting of a left T4N2 colon cancer, without other reported sites. The presence of limited, potentially resectable extrahepatic disease (lungs) does not preclude a curative-intent strategy if all sites can be cleared. From a hepatobiliary perspective, the liver disease appears technically resectable. This situation is considered potentially resectable in a multimodal, sequential curative strategy, provided both hepatic and pulmonary disease are amenable to complete treatment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and lung lesions.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Thoracic surgical assessment of pulmonary nodules is required.
• Given the high CEA level (620 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Initial systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Given synchronous extrahepatic disease and high CEA (620 ng/mL), initiate systemic douhlet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab)
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR).
• The objective is to assess tumor biology and confirm disease control at all sites.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and thoraco-abdominal enhanced CT-scan every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Sequential surgical strategy after response
• If disease control or response is observed:
	1.	Address the primary colon tumor if symptomatic or locally advanced : left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon primary) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) should be coordinated according to response and patient condition (ideally after liver surgery).
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for colectomy.

	2.	Perform parenchymal-sparing liver resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound : 
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to guide both resection and ablation.
• The goal is R0 resection while strictly preserving hepatic inflow/outflow.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.
	3.	Plan pulmonary metastasectomy or ablative treatment in a staged manner.
• The sequence (liver-first vs lung-first) depends on response and technical considerations.

E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of the liver metastases.
B. Resectability assessment of the pulmonary nodules by thoracic surgery.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Status and symptoms related to the primary colon tumor.
E. Patient’s performance status for staged surgical procedures.
F. Confirmation of absence of other extrahepatic disease on full staging.
G. Grade of differentiation, MSS/ MSI mutation and molecular status of the primary cancer: influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, right colon adenocarcinoma, four liver metastases (1.5-3.8 cm) and nodular peritoneal involvement at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 950 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Hepato-peritoneal disease, not curable upfront, discussion of induction chemotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – The presence of nodular peritoneal disease makes curative surgery uncertain. Definitive judgment requires additional decisive information (e.g., peritoneal cancer index, extent of peritoneal involvement, feasibility of cytoreductive surgery/HIPEC, liver MRI to define segmental distribution, vascular contact, and future liver remnant volume). Until these data are obtained and disease response to induction chemotherapy is documented, resection cannot be performed upfront.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic induction chemotherapy (e.g., 6‑12 cycles of FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) to attempt down‑staging of liver metastases and control peritoneal implants.  
- Within 2–3 weeks of starting chemotherapy, obtain a high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to delineate lesion location, vascular/biliary involvement, and calculate the standardized future liver remnant (FLR) ratio.  
- Perform a diagnostic laparoscopy (or staging laparoscopy) after 2–3 cycles of chemotherapy to assess peritoneal disease directly, record the Peritoneal Cancer Index (PCI), and determine whether complete cytoreduction is feasible.  
- If PCI is low (≤10–12) and complete cytoreduction appears achievable, plan a staged approach:  
   • Stage 1 – liver‑first hepatectomy (parenchymal‑sparing or two‑stage/ALPPS if FLR <30 %).  
   • Stage 2 – after hepatic recovery (≥4–6 weeks), perform colorectal primary resection (if not already removed) and peritoneal cytoreductive surgery with HIPEC in the same operation or as a separate procedure, depending on intra‑operative findings.  
- If peritoneal disease is extensive (high PCI, unresectable implants) or liver lesions remain unresectable after chemotherapy, continue systemic therapy (consider adding targeted agents based on molecular phenotype once known) and treat with palliative intent; revisit surgical options only if a clear conversion to resectable status is achieved.  
- Throughout treatment, monitor CEA trend; a significant decline (e.g., >50 % from baseline) supports continued aggressive approach, whereas rising CEA suggests progression and may shift to palliative management.  

Step 3 – Missing data (most crucial for decision‑making)  
- Detailed hepatic anatomy: segments involved, vascular or biliary invasion, arterial anatomy, and FLR ratio.  
- Liver MRI results (to confirm technical resectability).  
- Status of the colorectal primary (resected or still in situ, symptomatology).  
- Molecular phenotype of the tumor (RAS/BRAF status) to guide targeted systemic therapy.  
- Comprehensive peritoneal assessment: Total and regional Peritoneal Cancer Index, specific sites involved, involvement of hepatic ligaments, and FDG‑PET/CT to rule out occult disease.  
- Prior systemic treatment history (has any chemotherapy already been given?).  

These missing elements directly determine whether a curative‑intent hepatic and/or peritoneal resection is feasible after induction therapy.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with four liver metastases (1.5–3.8 cm) associated with nodular peritoneal involvement on CT. The presence of peritoneal carcinomatosis indicates systemic dissemination beyond the liver and precludes a curative hepatobiliary surgical approach at this stage. According to oncologic criteria, this situation is considered potentially resectable after a major conversion.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and peritoneal lesions.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Given the high CEA level (950 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Induction systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) according to MDT decision to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control according to patient tolerance.
• This allows treatment of potential micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology before surgery.
• The goal is to evaluate tumor biology and potential response at both hepatic and peritoneal sites.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and thoraco-abdominal enhanced CT-scan every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgical strategy
• Surgical re-evaluation may be considered only in the rare situation of major response with near-complete control of peritoneal disease and limited residual liver lesions.
• If disease control or response is observed:
	1.	Perform parenchymal-sparing liver resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound : 
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to guide both resection and ablation.
• The goal is R0 resection while strictly preserving hepatic inflow/outflow.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.
2. Address the primary colon tumor if symptomatic or locally advanced : start with laparoscopic assessment to evaluate PCI score and consider en-bloc right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with cytoreductive surgery (i.e. excision of all peritoneal nodules) with or without HIPEC according to response and patient condition.
• The sequence (primary first vs liver-first) depends on technical considerations and necessity of HIPEC.

E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

F. If disease remains disseminated
• Continue systemic second-line chemotherapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Extent and distribution of peritoneal disease on imaging.
B. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of liver lesions.
C. Molecular profile to optimize systemic treatment.
D. Status and symptoms related to the primary colon tumor.
E. Evolution of CEA and radiologic response over time.
F. Patient’s performance status for staged surgical procedures.
G. Confirmation of absence of other extrahepatic disease on full staging.
H. Grade of differentiation, MSS/ MSI mutation and molecular status of the primary cancer: influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
I. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 54 years old, mid-rectal T3N1 tumor with five bilobar liver metastases and a right lung metastasis at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. RAS wild-type, CEA 330 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Limited hepato-pulmonary involvement, evaluation of a possible combined approach.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: the case lacks decisive technical information required to confirm an R0 hepatic resection with adequate functional liver remnant. Specifically, the maximum and minimum lesion diameters, hepatic segments involved, vascular or biliary invasion, and the calculated future liver remnant (FLR) ratio are all marked as Missing. In addition, a liver‑specific MRI and confirmation of any prior systemic therapy are absent. Because these missing data directly determine whether all five bilobar metastases can be removed safely, the patient cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront” and does not meet criteria for “Not resectable” (no overt contraindication such as >70 % liver volume required or unresectable vascular involvement is documented). Therefore the disease is deemed potentially resectable pending completion of the missing assessments and/or down‑staging therapy.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Complete staging work‑up  
  • Obtain a contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (including hepatobiliary phase) to define lesion size, segmental distribution, vascular/biliary contact and to perform volumetric FLR calculation.  
  • Perform high‑resolution chest CT review (or PET‑CT) to characterize the right‑lung nodule (size, number, relation to bronchi/vessels) and assess mediastinal/hilar nodes.  
  • Obtain brain MRI (Missing item) to exclude occult CNS disease.  
  • Conduct pulmonary function tests to ensure fitness for possible pulmonary metastasectomy.  

- Systemic induction therapy  
  • Start a 3‑4 month oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX) combined with an anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab) given RAS wild‑type status, aiming for tumor shrinkage and biological selection.  
  • Monitor CEA trend and radiologic response after every two cycles (RECIST).  

- Re‑assessment after chemotherapy  
  • Repeat liver MRI and chest imaging. If lesions have responded sufficiently and FLR ≥30 % (or >0.5 % body‑weight ratio) is confirmed, proceed to hepatic surgery.  
  • If FLR is insufficient, plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy (e.g., right‑portal embolization followed by right‑hepatectomy and left‑lateral resection).  

- Sequence of operations  
  • Liver‑first approach: Perform hepatic resection (or combined resection/ablation) first because the rectal primary is asymptomatic and the liver surgery benefits from low central venous pressure without risking anastomotic compromise.  
  • Rectal primary: After hepatic surgery and recovery (≈4–6 weeks), deliver short‑course radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy) or total‑neoadjuvant therapy (TNT) followed by total mesorectal excision (TME) with a diverting stoma as needed.  
  • Pulmonary metastasis: If the right‑lung lesion is solitary and technically resectable, schedule video‑assisted thoracoscopic wedge resection either synchronously with the liver operation (if operative time and physiologic reserve allow) or as a staged procedure after hepatic recovery.  

- Adjuvant/maintenance therapy  
  • Continue postoperative systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 3‑6 months of FOLFOX or CAPOX) to eradicate micrometastatic disease.  
  • Consider maintenance anti‑EGFR therapy based on response and tolerance.  

- Surveillance  
  • CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced CT of chest/abdomen every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually; MRI liver if any equivocal findings.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Precise size of each liver metastasis (Maximum/Minimum Lesion Diameter).  
- Exact hepatic segments involved and presence of vascular or biliary invasion.  
- Calculated future liver remnant (FLR) ratio.  
- Results of a liver‑specific MRI (currently Missing).  
- Confirmation of any prior systemic chemotherapy (Missing).  
- Detailed characteristics of the lung metastasis (size, number, lobar distribution, relationship to bronchi/vessels).  
- Pulmonary function test results and brain imaging status.  
These items are essential to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with five bilobar liver metastases and a single right lung metastasis in the setting of a mid-rectal T3N1 tumor, without other reported sites. Limited, potentially resectable extrahepatic disease (lung) does not contraindicate a curative-intent strategy if all sites can be completely treated. From a hepatobiliary perspective, the liver disease may be amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections provided adequate future liver remnant is preserved. This situation is considered potentially resectable within a multimodal, sequential curative strategy.

A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver and pelvic MRI and chest CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and lung lesions.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Thoracic surgical assessment of the lung metastasis is required.
• Pelvic MRI to integrate rectal treatment planning.
• Given the high CEA level (330 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

• Start systemic doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status).
• The objective is to assess tumor biology and confirm disease control at hepatic and pulmonary sites.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver and pelvic MRI, and thoraco-abdominal enhanced CT-scan every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:
– Significant reduction in lesion size and number in both liver and lung.
– Feasibility of staged or parenchymal-sparing resections with adequate future liver remnant.

E. Potential surgical strategies for liver metastases if response is favorable
• Two-stage hepatectomy or combined parenchymal-sparing resections depending on response pattern.
• Portal vein embolization / venous deprivation / ALPPS may be required if major hepatectomy becomes necessary.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. Management of the rectal primary
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy with chemotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor

• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

• Plan pulmonary metastasectomy or ablative treatment in a staged manner.
• Preoperative evaluation of respiratory function

• Continue second-line systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.
• Continue systemic third-line chemotherapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

B. Resectability assessment of the lung lesion by thoracic surgery.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Detailed pelvic MRI to plan rectal treatment.
E. Patient’s performance status for staged multimodal procedures.
F. Confirmation of absence of other extrahepatic disease on full staging.
G. Evolution of CEA and radiologic response over time.
