Case_Content:
Man, 62 years old, left colon cancer with six liver metastases and lymph node involvement of the hepatic pedicle at the abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated, CEA 780 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Liver involvement associated with extra-hepatic lymph nodes, unfavorable prognosis.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has six hepatic metastases and radiologically documented hepatic‑pedicle lymph‑node involvement, which is an adverse prognostic factor and may limit curative intent surgery. Critical technical data are missing (maximum lesion size, hepatic segments involved, vascular or biliary invasion, and especially the future liver remnant [FLR] ratio). Moreover, the primary colorectal tumor has not been reported as resected, and no systemic therapy has yet been given. Because these missing items directly determine whether an R0 liver resection with adequate FLR can be achieved, the case cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront.” The necessary prerequisite actions are (a) systemic conversion chemotherapy and (b) completion of full staging (liver MRI, thoracic CT, PET‑CT, FLR calculation). If these steps lead to tumor down‑staging and an adequate FLR, resection may become feasible.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Initiate systemic conversion chemotherapy appropriate for KRAS‑mutated disease (e.g., mFOLFOX + bevacizumab).  
• Re‑stage after 2–3 cycles (or after 6 cycles) with:  
   – Contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or CT with volumetry) to define lesion size, segmental distribution, vascular/biliary involvement, and calculate FLR.  
   – Thoracic CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude occult pulmonary metastases.  
   – Dedicated imaging of the hepatic‑pedicle nodes (size, vascular relationship) and consider FDG‑PET for metabolic assessment.  
• If imaging shows sufficient tumor response and FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 0.5 % body‑weight), proceed to curative‑intent liver surgery.  
   – When FLR is borderline, perform portal‑vein embolization (PVE) or consider a two‑stage hepatectomy/ALPPS to induce hypertrophy.  
   – Plan resection of all hepatic lesions with negative margins (R0) and include resection of involved hepatic‑pedicle nodes if they are limited to the hepatoduodenal‑retropancreatic area and can be removed with clear margins.  
• Decide sequencing of primary‑tumor and liver surgery:  
   – If the colon primary is asymptomatic and no obstruction/perforation, adopt a liver‑first approach (hepatectomy first, then colectomy) to avoid compromising hepatic inflow/outflow.  
   – If the primary becomes symptomatic during chemotherapy, address it first (primary‑first).  
• After hepatic (and colorectal) resection, resume adjuvant chemotherapy for at least 6 months, tailored to response and tolerability.  
• Enroll the patient in close postoperative surveillance (CEA, cross‑sectional imaging every 3–4 months) to detect recurrence early.

Step 3 – Missing data  
• Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio and volumetric assessment.  
• Detailed hepatic metastasis characteristics: maximum diameter, segmental involvement, vascular/biliary contact.  
• Status of the primary colorectal tumor (resected or not, presence of obstruction/perforation/bleeding).  
• Results of thoracic imaging (CT or PET) to rule out pulmonary disease.  
• FDG‑PET scan for comprehensive staging of extra‑hepatic nodes.  
• Size, number and vascular relationships of the hepatic‑pedicle lymph nodes.  
• Whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been administered and the tumor’s response to it.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with six liver metastases associated with lymph node involvement of the hepatic pedicle. The presence of extrahepatic nodal disease at the hepatic hilum reflects systemic dissemination and markedly unfavorable tumor biology. Even if the liver lesions were technically resectable, the oncologic context precludes a curative hepatobiliary surgical approach at this stage. This situation is therefore considered potentially resectable from a hepatobiliary perspective.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and thoraco-abdominal CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of liver lesions and other para-aortic enlarged lymph nodes and a chest CT scan
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Given the high CEA level (780 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Systemic therapy as primary strategy (mandatory)
• Initiate or adapt systemic chemotherapy according to MDT decision (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab;
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR).
• The objective is global disease control and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Radiologic reassessment after treatment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI and abdominal CT after 2–3 months to reassess liver disease and nodal involvement.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of response.

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgery (highly exceptional)
• Surgical re-evaluation could be considered only in case of major response with major regression of nodal disease and significant downsizing of liver lesions.
• Any surgical strategy would remain highly selected and dependent on sustained disease control.

E. Surgical management of liver metastases (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform multiple wedge/segmental resections or ablation guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Perform en-bloc lymphadenectomy of the hepatic pedicles 
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. Management of the primary tumor
• If the sigmoid tumor has not yet been resected, a simultaneous sigmoid colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis can be considered, provided the patient’s condition allows combined surgery.
• Otherwise, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.

G. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

A. Presence of potential extra-hepatic involvement on 18FDG PET-CT.
B. Detailed liver MRI describing vascular and biliary relationships of each lesion.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy.
D. a chest CT scan

F. Status and symptoms related to the primary colon tumor.

Case_Content:
Woman, 70 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer, multiple bilobar liver metastases and a single cerebellar metastasis at the total body CT scan. CEA 860 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Systemic disease with brain involvement, neurological priority indication.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
• The patient has a right‑sided T4N2 primary that has not yet been removed (Primary Tumor Post‑Resection Characterization = Missing).  
• Liver disease is described only as “multiple bilobar metastases” with no data on number, size, vascular involvement or future‑liver‑remnant (FLR) volume (all items under Liver Metastases Characterization and FLR Ratio Compatibility Surgery are Missing).  
• A single cerebellar metastasis is present (Extrahepatic Brain Involvement = True). Current MDT notes give the brain lesion neurological priority, indicating that it must be treated before any curative‑intent surgery.  
Because (a) the brain metastasis requires local therapy first and (b) the hepatic burden cannot be judged without imaging, volumetry and response to systemic therapy, immediate curative resection of all disease is not feasible. The case therefore meets the definition of “potentially resectable” – resection will be possible only after (i) definitive treatment of the brain lesion and (ii) systemic chemotherapy (or targeted therapy) that down‑sizes the liver disease and allows an adequate FLR to be confirmed.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Urgent management of the cerebellar metastasis – stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) or microsurgical resection, depending on lesion size, edema and mass effect (Extrahepatic Brain Involvement details = Missing). This addresses the neurological priority identified by the MDT.  
2. Systemic therapy initiation – start a modern doublet chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) combined with a biologic agent (anti‑VEGF or anti‑EGFR) guided by molecular phenotype (RAS/BRAF/MSI status = Missing). Four to six cycles are recommended to assess tumor biology and achieve maximal response (see scenario 4 in the literature excerpt).  
3. Restaging after 2–3 months – obtain high‑quality contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or CT) and repeat thoraco‑abdominal imaging to define:  
   • Number, maximal diameter, segmental distribution, vascular/biliary involvement of liver metastases;  
   • Calculate FLR (target ≥ 30 % of total liver volume or >0.5 % body‑weight).  
   This information resolves the multiple “Missing” items under Liver Metastases Characterization and FLR Ratio.  
4. Decision point based on response  
   • If liver disease becomes resectable (R0 possible, adequate FLR, no major vascular invasion) – proceed with a liver‑first approach: perform staged hepatectomy (single‑stage if FLR sufficient, or two‑stage/ALPPS/portal vein embolization if FLR inadequate).  
   • If the primary colon tumor is symptomatic (obstruction, perforation, bleeding – all currently Missing) or remains bulky after chemotherapy, schedule a right hemicolectomy either before liver surgery (if liver disease is limited) or after liver resection (liver‑first strategy).  
5. Post‑hepatectomy/colon surgery – continue adjuvant systemic therapy (additional 4–6 cycles) to eradicate microscopic disease and address any residual extra‑hepatic burden.  
6. Surveillance – regular CEA monitoring (baseline 860 ng/mL) and imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–4 months for the first two years, with repeat brain imaging if neurologic symptoms recur.

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
- Detailed liver metastasis profile: exact number of lesions, maximal size, segmental involvement, relationship to major vessels/biliary structures, and presence of necrosis or calcifications.  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) volume and functional assessment.  
- Molecular phenotype of the primary tumor (RAS, BRAF, MSI status) to select the optimal biologic agent.  
- Status of the primary colon tumor (already resected or not) and any obstructive/bleeding/perforation symptoms.  
- Precise characteristics of the cerebellar lesion (size, edema, mass effect) to decide between surgery and stereotactic radiosurgery.

Man, 55 years old, rectosigmoid tumor, four liver metastases and pelvic peritoneal implants at the abdominal CT scan. BRAF wild-type, CEA 320 ng/mL.

Classification: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: The patient has four liver metastases and documented pelvic peritoneal implants, indicating synchronous extra‑hepatic disease. Current imaging (abdominal CT) does not provide essential technical details required to confirm hepatic resectability – hepatic segments involved, maximal lesion size, vascular or biliary involvement, and the future liver remnant (FLR) ratio are all missing. Moreover, the primary rectosigmoid tumor has not been reported as resected, and the extent of peritoneal disease (PCI) is unknown. Because these missing pieces are decisive for surgical feasibility, the case cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront.” The presence of potentially resectable liver disease (≤4 lesions) and limited peritoneal disease (pelvic only, no ascites) makes conversion after systemic therapy plausible, fulfilling the definition of “Potentially resectable.”  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  

1. Initial systemic therapy – Begin a standard doublet chemotherapy regimen (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) with bevacizumab, given the high CEA (320 ng/mL) and synchronous disease burden. Aim for 3–4 cycles, then restage.  

2. Restaging work‑up – After initial chemotherapy obtain:  
   - Multiphasic liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to define lesion size, segmental distribution, vascular/biliary contact, and calculate FLR.  
   - FDG‑PET/CT to confirm the extent of peritoneal disease and exclude occult pulmonary or nodal metastases.

3. Re‑assessment of resectability –  
   - If FLR ≥ 30 % (or >0.5 % body‑weight) and all hepatic lesions can be cleared with negative margins, proceed to a liver‑first (or “liver‑first”) approach.  
   - If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) before definitive resection.  

4. Surgical sequence –  
   a. Liver resection (major or minor depending on lesion distribution) performed first while the primary tumor remains in situ, provided the primary is asymptomatic.  
   b. Cytoreductive surgery (CRS) of peritoneal disease – if PCI is low (≤10) and complete macroscopic clearance is achievable, perform CRS in the same operation or as a second stage; HIPEC may be offered only within a clinical trial or after multidisciplinary discussion, as its benefit remains investigational.  
   c. Primary rectosigmoid resection – after hepatic and peritoneal surgery, perform a total mesorectal excision (TME) or low anterior resection, depending on tumor location and response.  

5. Adjuvant/continuation therapy – Resume systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) for 3–6 months post‑operatively, adjusting based on pathological response and postoperative recovery.  

6. Surveillance – Serial CEA measurements and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–4 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months up to 5 years.

Case_Content:
Woman, 66 years old, T3N1M1 transverse colon cancer, five liver metastases and two pulmonary nodules at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. RAS wild-type, CEA 420 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Bilateral hepato-pulmonary involvement, potentially treatable sequentially.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has five hepatic lesions and two pulmonary nodules. Technical resectability of the liver depends on (a) preservation of at least two contiguous liver segments with adequate inflow/outflow and biliary drainage, (b) an adequate future liver remnant (FLR ≥ 30 % in a normal liver), and (c) absence of major vascular or biliary invasion. The structured analysis lacks critical data on hepatic segmental distribution, maximum/minimum lesion diameters, vascular/biliary contact, and the FLR ratio. Likewise, the pulmonary nodules are not characterized for size, lobar distribution, or relationship to bronchi/vessels. Because these missing pieces are decisive for operative planning, the case cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront.” No contraindicating anatomic or functional factor is documented, so “Not resectable” is also inappropriate. The appropriate category is therefore “Potentially resectable,” pending completion of the missing assessments and/or neoadjuvant therapy to improve technical feasibility.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Baseline restaging – Obtain high‑quality liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast to define lesion size, segmental location, vascular/biliary involvement, and to calculate a precise FLR volume. Perform a thoracic PET‑CT (or at minimum a contrast‑enhanced chest CT with thin slices) to characterize the pulmonary nodules (size, metabolic activity, mediastinal/hilar nodes).  
2. Systemic therapy (induction) – Initiate a modern doublet chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) combined with a biologic agent appropriate for RAS‑wild‑type disease (e.g., anti‑EGFR such as cetuximab or panitumumab). Aim for 4–6 cycles, monitoring CEA trend and radiologic response. This serves to (a) assess tumor biology, (b) potentially downsize liver lesions, and (c) treat occult micrometastatic disease.  
3. Re‑assessment after induction – Repeat liver MRI and chest imaging. Re‑calculate FLR; if FLR remains <30 % after anticipated resection, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or an ALPPS/2‑stage approach to induce hypertrophy.  
4. Surgical sequencing –  
   • If the primary transverse colon tumor is asymptomatic and resectable: plan a “liver‑first” strategy (reverse sequence). After confirming that all hepatic disease can be removed with negative margins while preserving adequate FLR, perform parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy (segmental or non‑anatomic resections) possibly combined with intra‑operative ablation of lesions that are marginally resectable.  
   • If the primary tumor requires resection (obstruction, bleeding, or perforation risk) address it first or simultaneously with a limited hepatic resection, provided the operative risk remains acceptable.  
5. Pulmonary metastases – After hepatic surgery and recovery, re‑evaluate pulmonary nodules. If they remain limited (≤4 nodules, amenable to wedge resection or segmentectomy) and pulmonary reserve is adequate, proceed with staged thoracic metastasectomy (preferably video‑assisted thoracoscopic surgery). If pulmonary disease is borderline or patient comorbidity limits resection, consider stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) or percutaneous ablation as definitive local therapy.  
6. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy – Resume systemic chemotherapy (or switch to maintenance with fluoropyrimidine ± anti‑EGFR) after completion of all surgical procedures, guided by postoperative pathology and response.  
7. Surveillance – Serial CEA measurements and cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI of abdomen, CT of chest) every 3–4 months for the first 2 years, then at increasing intervals, to detect recurrence early.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- FLR ratio (volume) and liver volumetry  
- Liver MRI with detailed segmental and vascular assessment (size, number, vascular/biliary involvement)  
- Timing of liver metastases (synchronous vs metachronous)  
- Whether the colorectal primary has already been resected or is symptomatic (obstruction, perforation, bleeding)  
- Details of pulmonary nodules (size, lobar distribution, proximity to bronchi/vessels, mediastinal/hilar nodes)  
- FDG‑PET status for both liver and lung lesions  
- Information on any systemic therapy already administered  
These items are essential to confirm technical resectability, to choose the optimal sequencing of surgery, and to tailor systemic therapy.

Case_Content:
Woman, 60 years old, T4N2 rectal tumor, six bilobar liver metastases, pulmonary micronodules at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 1250 ng/mL, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Extensive hepato-pulmonary involvement, not resectable upfront.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The structured analysis shows six bilobar liver metastases (NumberOfMetastases: 6) and pulmonary micronodules (ExtrahepaticPulmonaryInvolvement: True). According to the literature, patients with multiple bilobar CRLM and limited extra‑hepatic disease may become resectable after tumor downsizing and careful functional assessment (HPB 2013; European J Surg Onc 2025). The MDT already judged the case “not resectable upfront,” indicating that immediate surgery would violate the technical criteria (need for ≥2 contiguous liver segments, adequate inflow/outflow, and sufficient FLR). A specific prerequisite is therefore required: conversion systemic chemotherapy (and possibly radiotherapy for the rectal primary) followed by restaging imaging to determine tumor response, FLR volume, and pulmonary lesion resectability. Because this prerequisite can be defined, the case fits the “Potentially resectable” category rather than a default “Resectable upfront” or “Not resectable.”

Step 2 - Oncological and surgical sequence  
1. Induction systemic therapy – Start a conversion regimen appropriate for RAS‑wild‑type disease (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + anti‑EGFR antibody, or FOLFOX + bevacizumab) for 3–4 months.  
2. Concurrent total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT) for the rectal primary – Deliver long‑course chemoradiation (or induction chemotherapy followed by chemoradiation) as recommended for T4 rectal tumors, aiming for maximal down‑staging before any surgical step.  
3. Restaging after induction – Perform high‑resolution liver MRI (missing in the analysis) to define lesion size, segmental distribution, vascular/biliary involvement, and calculate the future liver remnant (FLR) volume. Repeat thoraco‑abdominal CT and obtain FDG‑PET to confirm pulmonary nodules as true metastases and to assess their number, size, and anatomic relationships.  
4. Assess resectability after response  
   - If FLR ≥ 30 % (or >0.5 % body‑weight) and no major vascular invasion, proceed to hepatic surgery.  
   - If FLR is insufficient, schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) or consider a two‑stage hepatectomy/ALPPS to induce hypertrophy.  
5. Liver‑first approach – Perform the hepatic resection first (major or staged according to response), aiming for R0 removal of all liver lesions while preserving ≥2 contiguous segments. Use intra‑operative ultrasound to detect occult disease.  
6. Management of pulmonary disease – After hepatic recovery, reassess lung nodules. If they are limited (≤4, peripheral, and resectable with adequate pulmonary reserve), perform thoracic metastasectomy (wedge or segmentectomy) preferably in the same hospitalization if patient fitness allows; otherwise, consider SBRT or radiofrequency ablation for lesions unsuitable for surgery.  
7. Definitive rectal surgery – Once liver and lung disease are controlled, complete the rectal primary with total mesorectal excision (low anterior resection or APR as dictated by sphincter involvement) 4–6 weeks after the last radiotherapy dose, following the TNT protocol.  
8. Adjuvant systemic therapy – Continue postoperative chemotherapy (e.g., 6 months total) based on the response achieved and pathological risk factors (T4, N2, high CEA).  
9. Surveillance – Serial CEA measurements and imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

Step 3 - Missing data most critical for decision‑making  
- Future Liver Remnant (FLR) ratio – needed to decide whether PVE or staged hepatectomy is required.  
- Liver lesion characteristics – maximum/minimum diameter, hepatic segments involved, vascular or biliary contact, and arterial anatomy to plan resection margins and technical feasibility.  
- Liver MRI – not performed; essential for accurate lesion mapping and FLR calculation.  
- Systemic therapy status – whether any chemotherapy has already been given; influences timing of further treatment and assessment of tumor biology.  
- Primary tumor status – has the rectal cancer been resected or is it symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding) that would dictate priority of surgery.  
- Pulmonary nodule details – number, size, lobar distribution, relationship to bronchi/vessels, and FDG‑PET confirmation to determine resectability versus need for ablative therapy.  
- Performance status/comorbidities – not reported but required to confirm fitness for major combined procedures.

Man, 58 years old, left colon cancer, liver metastases (segments IV, V, VIII) and confirmed right iliac bone metastasis at the abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Hepato-osseous involvement, priority systemic management.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
 The patient has synchronous liver metastases in segments IV, V and VIII and a confirmed right iliac bone metastasis. Presence of extra‑hepatic disease (bone) makes curative hepatic resection unsafe until the bone lesion is shown to be controllable (e.g., by stereotactic radiotherapy, surgical fixation or proven stable disease).  
 The structured analysis lacks critical information that directly determines feasibility:  
  – Number, size and vascular/biliary involvement of the liver lesions (needed to judge whether an R0 resection is technically possible).  
  – Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio (required to confirm that the remaining liver will be sufficient).  
  – Detailed characteristics of the bone lesion (type, fracture risk, epidural/foraminal extension).  
 Because these decisive data are missing and because the MDT has already prioritized systemic therapy, the case cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront”. The prerequisite actions are (a) initiation of systemic chemotherapy with response assessment, and (b) definitive imaging/assessment of both liver disease (MRI, FLR calculation) and bone lesion. If these steps demonstrate disease control and adequate FLR, surgery can be pursued – hence “Potentially resectable”.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Systemic induction therapy  
    Start an oxaliplatin‑based doublet (e.g., CAPOX or FOLFOX) combined with bevacizumab, because the tumor is KRAS‑mutated (anti‑EGFR agents are ineffective).  
    Plan 3–6 cycles; hold bevacizumab 6–8 weeks before any planned liver surgery to reduce bleeding risk.  

2. Baseline and interim imaging  
    Obtain a thoraco‑CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary metastases.  
    Perform a high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to define number, size, vascular contact, and to calculate FLR.  
    Re‑image the iliac bone lesion with MRI/CT and consider a bone scan or PET to characterize lesion type and assess stability.  

3. Re‑assessment after induction  
    If liver lesions have shrunk sufficiently (e.g., ≤3 cm each, no major vascular invasion) and FLR is ≥30 % (or ≥0.5 % body weight), proceed to surgical planning.  
    If the bone metastasis is solitary, stable, and amenable to local control (e.g., stereotactic body radiotherapy or surgical fixation), treat it now; otherwise, continue systemic therapy and consider it a non‑curative situation.  

4. Surgical sequencing (reverse/liver‑first approach)  
    Stage 1 – Hepatectomy: Perform a right‑extended hepatectomy (segments IV‑VIII) aiming for R0 margins. If FLR is borderline, schedule portal vein embolization before resection.  
    Stage 2 – Primary colon resection: After hepatic recovery (≈6 weeks), resect the left‑sided primary tumor (segmental colectomy) unless obstructive symptoms develop earlier, in which case combine with liver surgery (simultaneous) if the hepatic resection is limited.  

5. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy  
    Resume the same systemic regimen (or switch to FOLFIRI + bevacizumab if progression) for 4–6 months post‑operatively.  
    Consider postoperative radiotherapy to the iliac bone if not previously treated and if the lesion remains viable.  

6. Follow‑up  
    CEA and imaging (CT/MRI) every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.  

Step 3 – Missing data (most crucial for decision‑making)

 Details of the bone lesion: histology/osteolytic vs. sclerotic, fracture risk, epidural/foraminal extension, and whether it has been treated.  
 Prior systemic therapy (has any chemotherapy already been given?).  

Acquiring these data will allow a definitive re‑assessment of resectability and refinement of the surgical plan.

Case_Content:
Woman, 69 years old, T3N1 rectal tumor with two liver metastases and an isolated left pulmonary nodule at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. RAS wild-type, CEA 210 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Limited hepato-pulmonary involvement, possibility of a combined approach depending on response.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- The patient has synchronous T3N1 rectal cancer, two liver metastases and a solitary left‑lung nodule.  Current imaging (CT) confirms disease but lacks critical anatomic detail (liver MRI, vascular/biliary involvement, segmental distribution, lesion size) that determines whether an R0 hepatic resection can be achieved while preserving ≥2 contiguous liver segments with adequate inflow/outflow and a sufficient future liver remnant (FLR).  The structured analysis lists FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery as “Missing”.  
- The primary colorectal tumor has not been reported as resected (Missing) and there is no information on whether neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy has been given.  Rectal cancer of T3N1 generally requires neoadjuvant therapy before definitive surgery; without this the primary may not be resectable or may compromise timing of liver surgery.  
- Systemic treatment status for both liver and pulmonary disease is unknown (Missing for liver, Assumed False for lung).  Current guidelines recommend upfront systemic chemotherapy for synchronous disease to assess tumor biology and potentially downsize metastases.  
Because these specific prerequisites (pre‑operative systemic therapy, detailed hepatic imaging, FLR assessment, and neoadjuvant treatment of the rectal primary) are required before a definitive surgical plan can be made, the case is classified as “Potentially resectable”.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Neoadjuvant phase  
   - Initiate standard peri‑operative systemic chemotherapy for metastatic disease (e.g., 6 cycles of FOLFOX ± bevacizumab, given RAS‑wild type).  Monitor CEA trend and perform restaging CT/MRI after 2–3 cycles to evaluate response of liver lesions and the pulmonary nodule.  
   - Concurrently deliver neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (or total‑neoadjuvant therapy) for the rectal primary according to current TNT protocols (e.g., 5‑FU‑based chemoradiation or induction chemotherapy followed by chemoradiation).  Restage the rectum with high‑resolution pelvic MRI 6–8 weeks after completion to assess down‑staging and circumferential margin status.  
   - Obtain a liver‑specific MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and diffusion sequences to define lesion size, segmental location, vascular/biliary involvement, and to calculate the FLR volume.  If FLR is <30 % (or <0.5 % of body weight), consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy strategy.  

2. Multidisciplinary reassessment (after neoadjuvant therapy and imaging)  
   - If liver lesions are now amenable to an R0 resection with adequate FLR, and the pulmonary nodule remains solitary, proceed to a curative‑intent surgical plan.  
   - If the lung nodule is PET‑avid or enlarges, obtain FDG‑PET/CT; if confirmed metastatic, plan for pulmonary metastasectomy (wedge resection) either synchronously with liver surgery or in a staged fashion, depending on operative risk and pulmonary reserve.  

3. Surgical sequence (tailored to patient fitness and anatomic considerations)  
   - Option A – Simultaneous approach (preferred when liver resection is limited, FLR adequate, and the rectal tumor is down‑staged to allow low anterior resection with a diverting stoma):  
        • First, perform laparoscopic/open liver resection of the two metastases (segmental or non‑anatomic resections) preserving ≥2 contiguous segments.  
        • Immediately thereafter, perform low anterior resection (TME) of the rectal primary.  
        • If intra‑operative assessment confirms the lung nodule is resectable and pulmonary function is acceptable, add a thoracoscopic wedge resection in the same operative session.  
   - Option B – Staged approach (if liver resection is major or FLR borderline):  
        • Stage 1: Hepatic resection (or combined resection + ablation) after confirming FLR adequacy.  
        • Stage 2 (4–6 weeks later, after recovery): Low anterior resection of the rectum.  
        • Stage 3 (after colorectal recovery, typically 4–6 weeks later): Thoracoscopic wedge resection of the left lung nodule.  
   - Throughout, employ intra‑operative ultrasound to detect occult liver disease and achieve negative margins (≥1 mm).  

4. Adjuvant therapy  
   - After completion of all resections and recovery, resume systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) for at least 3 months as adjuvant treatment, given the high initial CEA (210 ng/mL) and synchronous metastatic burden.  
   - Consider postoperative radiotherapy to the pelvis if the final pathology shows high‑risk features (e.g., positive circumferential margin, ypT4).  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Detailed hepatic anatomy: lesion size, segmental distribution, vascular/biliary contact, and liver MRI findings.  
- Quantitative FLR assessment (volume or ratio).  
- Status of the primary rectal tumor (whether already resected) and its response to neoadjuvant therapy (MRI restaging).  
- Confirmation of systemic chemotherapy already administered (if any) and its effect on tumor markers.  
- Full characterization of the pulmonary nodule (size, exact lobar location, FDG‑PET avidity, relationship to bronchi/vessels).  
- Grade of differentiation of the primary tumor (prognostic).  

These missing pieces are decisive for confirming technical resectability, planning the sequence of operations, and determining whether additional pre‑operative interventions (PVE, further chemotherapy, or radiotherapy) are required.

Man, 65 years old, right T4N2 colon cancer, eight bilobar liver metastases and moderate peritoneal carcinomatosis at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 970 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Extensive hepato-peritoneal disease, goal of systemic control.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Not resectable: The patient has eight bilobar liver metastases and moderate peritoneal carcinomatosis on abdominal CT. Bilobar disease with this tumor burden makes an R0 liver resection unlikely, and the presence of peritoneal carcinomatosis indicates extra‑hepatic disease that, in its current extent, precludes curative‑intent hepatic surgery. Moreover, critical technical data (future liver remnant ratio, vascular/biliary involvement, lesion size) are missing, further supporting the conclusion that an upfront resection would not achieve oncologically adequate margins while preserving liver function.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy with an intensive regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) aiming for tumor down‑staging and assessment of disease biology.  
- Obtain baseline molecular profiling of the primary tumor (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MSI‑H/dMMR) to guide targeted agents and prognostication.  
- Perform comprehensive restaging after 2–3 months of therapy: contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or CT if MRI unavailable), thoraco‑CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary disease, and repeat abdominal CT to re‑evaluate peritoneal disease and calculate the future liver remnant volume.  
- Re‑assess resectability after systemic therapy: if liver burden is sufficiently reduced (e.g., <4 lesions, adequate FLR ≥ 30 % of standardized liver volume) and peritoneal disease is limited (low Peritoneal Cancer Index, no ascites), consider a staged curative approach—either (a) two‑stage hepatectomy with portal vein embolization or ALPPS, or (b) simultaneous colorectal resection and liver resection if the primary tumor becomes resectable and the liver surgery is limited to ≤3 segments.  
- If disease does not respond adequately or progresses, continue systemic therapy (potentially switching to second‑line regimen) and consider palliative measures, including possible cytoreductive surgery with HIPEC only if peritoneal disease becomes limited and the patient remains fit.  
- Throughout treatment, monitor CEA trends (baseline 970 ng/mL) as a surrogate for response and adjust therapy accordingly.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio and volumetric assessment.  
- Maximum and minimum diameters of each liver lesion; segmental distribution.  
- Presence of vascular or biliary invasion by liver metastases.  
- Molecular phenotype of the primary tumor (KRAS/NRAS/BRAF status, MSI‑H/dMMR).  
- Timing of liver metastases (synchronous vs. metachronous).  
- Status of the primary colorectal tumor (resected or not, presence of obstruction/perforation/bleeding).  
- Detailed peritoneal disease assessment: Peritoneal Cancer Index, sites involved, involvement of hepatic ligaments, presence of ascites.  
- Thoraco‑CT or PET‑CT results to exclude pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic metastases.  
- Patient’s performance status, comorbidities, and liver function tests (to gauge tolerance of chemotherapy and potential surgery).  
These missing elements are pivotal for refining resectability judgments and tailoring the subsequent multimodal treatment plan.

Case_Content:
Man, 59 years old, left T3N1M1 colon tumor, five bilobar liver metastases (1.5-3.5 cm). CEA 1150 ng/mL. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.Liver MRI: contact of segment VIII lesion with middle hepatic vein.
MDT Discussion: Technically resectable disease, high tumor marker suggests systemic risk.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: The MDT notes that the liver disease is technically resectable, but several oncologic and functional factors preclude an immediate operation. (a) A very high CEA (1150 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation place the patient in a high‑risk biologic category, which in the literature is an indication for neoadjuvant systemic therapy before surgery. (b) Bilobar distribution of five lesions (1.5‑3.5 cm) with vascular contact to the middle hepatic vein requires confirmation that an R0 resection can be achieved while preserving adequate inflow/outflow and a sufficient future liver remnant (FLR). (c) Critical information required for definitive surgical planning – FLR volume, extra‑hepatic disease status (chest/abdomen CT), and whether the primary colon tumour has already been resected – is currently missing. Because a specific prerequisite (neoadjuvant chemotherapy and FLR assessment) and a decisive missing piece of information (extra‑hepatic staging) are identified, the case fits the “Potentially resectable” category.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Complete staging – obtain a contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal, bone or brain metastases that were not documented.  
2. Functional liver assessment – perform CT‑based volumetry (or MRI) to calculate the FLR ratio; if FLR < 30 % (or < 20 % in a compromised liver), plan portal vein embolisation (PVE) or a two‑stage/hepatectomy‑assisted approach.  
3. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy – start a KRAS‑mutant‑appropriate regimen (e.g., FOLFOX ± bevacizumab or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) for 2–3 months. The goal is to (i) obtain a “proof of time” for tumor biology, (ii) attempt down‑staging of the lesions, and (iii) treat any occult micrometastatic disease.  
4. Re‑assessment after chemotherapy – repeat liver MRI (including vascular phase) and FLR volumetry; confirm that the segment VIII lesion still only contacts the middle hepatic vein and that a negative‑margin resection is feasible.  
5. Surgical sequencing –  
   • If the primary colon tumour is still in situ and asymptomatic, adopt a “liver‑first” strategy after chemotherapy response, because liver disease is the limiting factor.  
   • Perform a staged hepatectomy tailored to the distribution: for example, right hepatectomy (including segment VIII) with preservation of the middle hepatic vein or a parenchyma‑sparing non‑anatomic resection of the segment VIII lesion combined with left‑lateral resections to achieve R0 margins while leaving ≥ 2 contiguous segments.  
   • If FLR is marginal, consider a two‑stage approach (right portal vein embolisation → hypertrophy → second‑stage resection) or ALPPS, depending on centre expertise.  
6. Primary tumour resection – after hepatic clearance (or concurrently if the primary is symptomatic), perform a standard left‑sided colectomy with adequate lymphadenectomy.  
7. Adjuvant therapy – continue postoperative systemic chemotherapy (same backbone as neoadjuvant) for a total of 6 months of peri‑operative treatment, adjusting based on pathological response and postoperative recovery.  
8. Surveillance – serial CEA measurements and imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–4 months for the first 2 years, then at increasing intervals, given the high baseline CEA and aggressive biology.

Step 3 – Missing data (most crucial for final decision)  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) volume/ratio.  
- Results of thoraco‑abdominal imaging to confirm absence or presence of extra‑hepatic metastases.  
- Timing of liver metastases (synchronous vs. metachronous).  
- Whether the primary colon tumour has already been resected and its pathological grade.  
- Detailed arterial/portal venous anatomy and extent of vascular involvement beyond “contact” with the middle hepatic vein.  
- Performance status and comorbidities (cardiopulmonary fitness for major hepatectomy).  
- Any systemic therapy already administered and the tumour’s response to it.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with five bilobar liver metastases (1.5–3.5 cm), including a segment VIII lesion in contact with the middle hepatic vein, without reported extrahepatic disease. From a technical standpoint, complete clearance with parenchymal-sparing resections appears feasible while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is potentially resectable. However, the very high CEA level (1150 ng/mL) suggests aggressive tumor biology and a high systemic risk.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to confirm the relationship of the 5 lesions to segment VIII vascular and biliary structures. Precise anatomical mapping is required to plan a safe parenchymal-sparing resection and a chest CT scan
• Given the high CEA level (1150 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Preoperative systemic therapy
• The elevated CEA level (1150 ng/mL) and multiplicity of lesions suggest biologically active disease.
• Give 3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) to treat potential micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology.
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• This period treats micrometastatic disease and evaluates tumor biology.

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and evaluate vascular/biliary relationships.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

D. Surgical management (staged strategy)
• If restaging confirms continued resectability, perform a first multiple atypical resection for the 5 lesions and/or segmentectomy 8 with en-bloc partial resection a the middle hepatic veine removing the 5 metastases, or a formal right hepatectomy if anatomically more appropriate, and if volume of the remnant liver is sufficient, aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin .
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.
• After recovery, perform left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis 

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals given the elevated initial tumor marker (CEA 1150 ng/mL).

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy. 
B. Precise segmental distribution of the three lesions within the left liver and detailed vascular/biliary relationship of the liver lesion – essential to confirm that a non anatomic resection will achieve clear margins without compromising hepatic inflow/outflow.

In addition, the primary colorectal tumor has not been documented as resected, which influences the sequencing of surgery. These gaps require further imaging (liver MRI) and functional assessment before an upfront hepatectomy can be safely planned.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Obtain a high‑resolution liver MRI (or contrast‑enhanced triphasic CT) to define segmental location, vascular/biliary involvement, and to calculate the FLR volume.  
- Perform a PET‑CT (or brain MRI) to exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease, particularly brain metastasis, which is currently missing.  
- Clarify whether the transverse colon primary has been resected; if not, schedule a curative‑intent colectomy (either before or simultaneous with liver surgery depending on tumor location and patient fitness).  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy tailored to RAS/BRAF wild‑type disease (e.g., FOLFOX ± cetuximab) for 2–3 months to assess tumor biology (“proof of time”) and to potentially downsize the hepatic lesions. Monitor CEA trends; a falling CEA would support favorable biology.  
- Re‑stage after chemotherapy with repeat MRI; if FLR ≥30 % (or ≥20 % in a non‑cirrhotic liver) and no vascular/biliary encasement is present, proceed to curative‑intent liver resection aiming for R0 margins (anatomical or non‑anatomical resections preserving at least two contiguous segments). Consider portal vein embolization if FLR is borderline.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (same regimen) for approximately 6 months, followed by regular CEA surveillance and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–6 months.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio and volumetric assessment.  
- Precise hepatic segments involved and any vascular or biliary contact/invasion.  
- Results of a liver‑specific MRI (or equivalent high‑quality imaging).  
- Confirmation of whether the primary transverse colon tumor has already been resected.  
- Timing of liver metastases (synchronous vs metachronous) to inform prognosis.  
- Information on any systemic therapy already administered.  
- Status of extra‑hepatic brain involvement (brain MRI/PET‑CT).

Case_Content:
Woman, 60 years old, left T4N1M1 colon cancer, six liver metastases (up to 5.6 cm) at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 1400 ng/mL. KRAS G12C mutation confirmed.
MDT Discussion: Specific molecular profile, may benefit from a later targeted strategy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: Six liver metastases (≥5 lesions) with a largest diameter of 5.6 cm place the disease in the borderline‑to‑unresectable range. Definitive technical resectability cannot be confirmed without (a) a quantified future liver remnant (FLR) ratio, (b) precise mapping of hepatic segments involved and any vascular or biliary contact, and (c) confirmation that no extra‑hepatic disease (especially pulmonary) is present. These missing items are decisive for surgical feasibility; therefore resection must be preceded by further imaging, functional liver assessment and likely conversion chemotherapy.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- 1. Obtain complete staging:  
   • Perform thoracic CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude pulmonary metastases.  
   • Perform liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast to delineate segmental distribution, vascular/biliary involvement, and to calculate FLR volume.  
- 2. Assess liver functional reserve:  
   • Use CT‑volumetry or MRI‑volumetry to calculate FLR; if FLR < 30 % (or < 20 % in compromised liver), plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or consider a two‑stage hepatectomy/ALPPS.  
- 3. Systemic conversion therapy (first line):  
   • Initiate oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX) combined with bevacizumab (anti‑VEGF), because KRAS G12C precludes anti‑EGFR antibodies.  
   • Consider enrollment in a clinical trial of a KRAS G12C inhibitor (e.g., sotorasib) in combination with chemotherapy, given the molecular profile.  
   • Treat for 2–3 months (≈ 4–6 cycles), reassessing tumor burden after every 2 cycles.  
- 4. Response evaluation:  
   • Repeat liver MRI and CT to document size reduction and to re‑calculate FLR.  
   • If sufficient downsizing (e.g., reduction of lesions to ≤3 cm and/or decrease in number) and FLR becomes adequate, proceed to surgery.  
- 5. Surgical plan (if conversion achieved):  
   • Primary colon tumor: if not yet resected and asymptomatic, schedule simultaneous or staged colectomy after liver surgery; if symptomatic (obstruction/bleeding) address before or concurrently.  
   • Liver: aim for R0 resection of all hepatic lesions preserving at least two contiguous segments with adequate inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  
   • If FLR remains insufficient after downsizing, perform PVE followed by interval hypertrophy (≈ 4–6 weeks) then definitive hepatectomy; alternatively, employ a two‑stage hepatectomy if lesions are bilobar.  
- 6. Post‑operative adjuvant therapy:  
   • Continue the same systemic regimen (FOLFOX + bevacizumab) for 6 months if tolerated, then consider maintenance bevacizumab or enrollment in a KRAS G12C‑targeted maintenance trial.  
   • Monitor CEA and imaging every 3–4 months for the first 2 years.  

Step 3 – Missing data (most crucial for recommendation)  
- FLR ratio / liver volumetry (required to decide if immediate resection, PVE, or staged approach).  
- Detailed hepatic segment involvement and presence of vascular or biliary contact (affects technical feasibility).  
- Thoracic CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary metastases.  
- Liver MRI (for precise lesion characterization and volumetry).  
- Status of the primary colon tumor (resected vs. unresected, symptomatic vs. asymptomatic).  
- Whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been administered.  
- Assessment for other extra‑hepatic sites (bone, brain) that were not evaluated.

The patient presents with six liver metastases (up to 5.6 cm) in the context of a left T4N1 colon cancer and very high CEA (1400 ng/mL). The number, size, and likely bilobar distribution of lesions make a safe R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant unlikely at this stage. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable after major conversion.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships.
• Given the high CEA level (1400 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Systemic therapy as primary strategy (mandatory)
• Initiate intensive systemic chemotherapy according to MDT decision (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).
• The presence of a KRAS G12C mutation is poor prognostic factor and may allow consideration of targeted strategies in later lines of therapy. 
• The objective is tumor downsizing and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Radiologic reassessment after treatment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 3-6 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgery (exceptional)
• Surgical re-evaluation could be considered only if a major radiologic and biologic response occurs with significant reduction in number and size of lesions allowing parenchymal-sparing resections.

E. Management of the primary tumor
• Consider transverse colectomy of right colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis if the tumor is symptomatic of if MDT propose intra-arterial chemotherapy.

F. If disease remains extensive
• Continue second-line systemic therapy and/or consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).
• If disease remains extensive, consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

A. Detailed vascular mapping on MRI to confirm absence of true portal invasion.
B. Future liver remnant (FLR) calculation in case of potential conversion.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
D. Presence or absence of extrahepatic disease on full staging.
E. Patient’s general condition and comorbidities influencing tolerance of combined surgery.
F. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA.
G. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
H. Status and symptoms related to the primary colon tumor.

Case_Content:
Man, 57 years old, low T3N2M1 rectal cancer, four peripheral liver metastases (2-3.5 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 90 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, MSS, positive circulating tumor cells.
MDT Discussion: Presence of circulating cells despite low volume, prognostic significance discussed.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The case reports four peripheral liver metastases (2–3.5 cm) but lacks critical anatomic details required to confirm technical feasibility (hepatic segments involved, vascular contact/invasion, FLR ratio, liver MRI). Moreover, the rectal primary (T3 N2) has not been resected and its symptom status is unknown, indicating that neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (or total‑neoadjuvant therapy) is required before any definitive surgery. Because a specific prerequisite (completion of neoadjuvant therapy and acquisition of detailed hepatic imaging) is missing, the lesions cannot be declared resectable upfront.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate total‑neoadjuvant therapy (TNT) for the rectal primary: short‑course radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy) followed by 6 cycles of FOLFOX (± anti‑EGFR antibody given RAS‑wild‑type) to treat both the primary and liver metastases.  
- Perform restaging after TNT with high‑resolution liver MRI (including diffusion‑weighted and hepatobiliary‑specific sequences) and repeat thoraco‑abdominal CT to define:  
   • exact hepatic segments harboring each metastasis,  
   • relationship to hepatic veins, portal/hepatic arteries, and biliary structures,  
   • calculation of future liver remnant (FLR) volume; if FLR < 30 % consider portal vein embolisation (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy.  
- Multidisciplinary reassessment:  
   • If liver disease is now technically resectable with an adequate FLR and no major vascular invasion, proceed to curative‑intent liver surgery.  
   • Choose surgical sequencing based on dominant disease:  
        – “Liver‑first” (reverse) approach is preferred because the liver disease is limited but requires major resection; this allows early control of metastases while the rectal primary is still responding to CRT.  
        – If liver resection can be performed as a minor hepatectomy and FLR is sufficient, a simultaneous liver‑resection plus low‑anterior resection (TME) can be considered to reduce overall treatment time.  
- After hepatic resection (R0 intended), complete the rectal surgery (TME) within 6–8 weeks, using sphincter‑preserving technique if oncologically safe (CRM > 1 mm).  
- Post‑operative adjuvant systemic therapy to complete a total of 12 cycles of FOLFOX (or switch to a maintenance regimen) and consider enrolment in a clinical trial for circulating tumor‑cell‑positive disease.

- Hepatic segments involved and presence of vascular or biliary invasion (LiverMetastasesCharacterization).  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio (FutureLiverRemnantFLRRatio).  
- Liver MRI results (ImagingExams – liver MRI).  
- Whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been administered (LiverMetastasesUnderSystemicTreatment).

• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define vascular and biliary relationships and calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

• Given the presence of circulating tumor cells indicating systemic dissemination risk, administer 2–3 months of induction chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status).
• The objective is treatment of micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Radiologic reassessment after treatment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 2-3 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

• Given the T3N2 rectal cancer, long-course radiotherapy is appropriate to optimize local control and allow coordinated surgical planning 

E. Coordinated surgical strategy
• Initiate doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX) during the waiting period following radiotherapy. This period treats potential micrometastatic disease and tests tumor biology.

• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins.

-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor

• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.

• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

B. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of the three liver lesions on MRI.

Woman, 72 years old, right T3N0M1 colon tumor, single 5.6 cm metastasis in segment VIII, in close contact with IVC at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 540 ng/mL, RAS wild-type.

Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Classification: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: The liver lesion is solitary and technically amenable to resection, but it is in close contact with the inferior vena cava, creating a major vascular concern. Critical information required to confirm feasibility is missing: (a) high‑resolution liver MRI (or MRCP) to delineate the exact relationship of the metastasis to the IVC and to define arterial anatomy; (b) assessment of the future liver remnant (FLR) volume and functional capacity; (c) confirmation that the primary colon tumor has been or can be safely resected. Until these data are obtained, and/or until neoadjuvant systemic therapy is given to test tumor biology and possibly downsize the lesion, definitive upfront surgery cannot be recommended.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Obtain a contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (including hepatobiliary phase) to clarify IVC involvement, arterial/portal anatomy, and to detect any occult hepatic lesions.  
• Perform volumetric CT or MRI to calculate FLR; if FLR is <30 % (or <0.5 % body‑weight ratio), plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or consider a two‑stage hepatectomy/ALPPS.  
• Initiate systemic chemotherapy now (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX plus anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody given RAS wild‑type) for 2–3 months. This serves to (i) assess disease biology, (ii) potentially shrink the 5.6 cm lesion away from the IVC, and (iii) treat micrometastatic disease.  
• Re‑image after chemotherapy (CT + MRI) to re‑evaluate vascular contact and FLR. If the lesion becomes resectable with a clear (>1 mm) margin and adequate liver remnant, proceed with a liver‑first approach:  
   – Perform an anatomical or non‑anatomical segment‑VIII resection (or extended right posterior sectionectomy) with intra‑operative ultrasound guidance, ensuring negative margins and preservation of inflow/outflow.  
   – If FLR is adequate, consider simultaneous right‑colon resection (right hemicolectomy) in the same operation; otherwise, schedule colon resection after hepatic recovery (interval 6–8 weeks).  
• Post‑operative management: continue adjuvant chemotherapy (total 6 months peri‑operative therapy) and monitor CEA serially.  
• If MRI shows unresectable IVC invasion or FLR remains insufficient despite PVE, shift to alternative local therapies (e.g., stereotactic body radiotherapy or percutaneous ablation) and continue systemic treatment.

Step 3 - Missing data  
• FLR volume and functional assessment (critical for surgical safety).  
• Liver MRI with vascular detail (necessary to decide whether IVC involvement is resectable or requires vascular reconstruction).  
• Status of the primary colon tumor (resected vs. pending) and any obstructive/bleeding symptoms.  
• Results of any pre‑operative systemic therapy already administered.  
• Arterial anatomy and presence of biliary involvement (to plan resection strategy).  
These items are essential to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.

• Obtain high resolution liver MRI to define exact segmental distribution of the lesion with detailed vascular and biliary relationships.

• After recovery, perform right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon cancer) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis.

• Continue systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.

• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis

Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: the case lacks several decisive pieces of information that are required before a definitive surgical plan can be made. Specifically, the status of the primary colorectal tumor (whether it has been resected), the exact number, size and segmental distribution of the liver lesions, the future liver remnant (FLR) volume, and the presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease on thoracic imaging are all missing. These items directly determine technical feasibility (adequate FLR, vascular/biliary involvement) and oncologic suitability (extra‑hepatic disease, primary tumor control). Until they are obtained, the patient cannot be classified as resectable upfront nor as unresectable.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Complete staging work‑up:  
  • Perform a thoraco‑CT scan to rule out pulmonary metastases (Missing in analysis).  
  • Obtain a contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with liver‑specific agents to define number, size, vascular contact and segmental involvement of the metastases (Missing).  
  • Calculate FLR by volumetric CT or MRI; if FLR <30 % (or <20 % in compromised liver) consider portal vein embolisation (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy (Information on FLRRatio is Missing).  
  • Confirm whether the primary left‑sided colon cancer has been resected; if not, assess for obstruction, perforation or bleeding (all Missing) and plan primary resection either before or simultaneously with liver surgery depending on symptomatology.  

- Systemic therapy initiation (neoadjuvant):  
  • Given the HER2 amplification, start a HER2‑targeted regimen (e.g., trastuzumab + pertuzumab or trastuzumab‑deruxtecan) combined with a standard doublet chemotherapy such as FOLFOX (or FOLFIRI) as recommended for HER2‑positive mCRC.  
  • Use the high CEA (2100 ng/mL) and bilateral disease as rationale for neoadjuvant treatment to obtain “proof of time” and assess tumor biology.  

- Re‑assessment after 2–3 months of systemic therapy:  
  • Repeat liver MRI (and thoracic CT) to evaluate response, down‑staging of lesions, and FLR adequacy.  
  • If sufficient tumor shrinkage and FLR ≥30 % are achieved, proceed to curative‑intent liver resection. Bilobar disease can be addressed with a staged approach (right‑first hepatectomy with PVE or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy – ALPPS) or with combined resection and ablative techniques for lesions in difficult locations.  

- Management of the primary tumor:  
  • If the primary remains in situ and is asymptomatic, a liver‑first strategy is acceptable; otherwise, perform simultaneous colon resection (low anterior resection or segmental colectomy) after confirming patient fitness.  

- Post‑operative plan:  
  • Continue HER2‑directed therapy for at least 6 months post‑resection (adjuvant phase) together with standard peri‑operative chemotherapy as tolerated.  
  • Serial CEA monitoring and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–6 months for surveillance.  

Step 3 - Missing data (most critical for decision‑making)  
- Primary tumor status: has it been resected? (Missing)  
- Primary tumor symptomatology: obstruction, perforation, bleeding (Missing)  
- Liver metastases details: number of lesions, maximum and minimum diameters, hepatic segments involved, vascular or biliary invasion (All Missing)  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio and volumetric assessment (Missing)  
- Thoraco‑CT results to exclude pulmonary metastases (Missing)  
- Liver MRI results for precise lesion characterization (Missing)  
- Timing of metastases (synchronous vs metachronous) (Missing)  
- Prior systemic therapy (type, cycles, response) (Missing)  
- Extra‑hepatic bone or brain involvement (Missing)  

Acquiring these data points will allow conversion of the “potentially resectable” classification to either “resectable upfront” or “not resectable” and will guide the precise surgical plan.

Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with multiple bilobar liver metastases and very high CEA (2100 ng/mL) in the context of a left colon cancer with HER2 amplification and BRAF wild-type status. The tumor burden and bilobar distribution preclude the possibility of achieving a complete R0 resection while preserving an adequate future liver remnant at this stage. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable after major conversion.

A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships and a chest CT scan
• Given the high CEA level (2100 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Consider short peri-operative systemic therapy
• Given the elevated CEA (2100 ng/mL) and HER2 positivity, a short course (2–3 months) of peri-operative systemic therapy adapted to the molecular profile should be considered to treat micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology.
• HER2-positive colorectal cancer (CRC), found in 2–6% of cases (mainly RAS wild-type and left-sided), is treated with targeted therapies like trastuzumab combined with tucatinib or trastuzumab deruxtecan. 

C. Radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 2–3 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

D. Surgical management after restaging
• If disease remains controlled, perform ultrasound-guided left lateral sectoriectomy (rection of segments II and III) aiming for R0 margins.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

E. Surgical management of the primary tumor
• After recovery, perform left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

G. If disease remains extensive
• Continue systemic and targeted therapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented management according to MDT.

A. Precise segmental distribution of the 2 lesions within the left liver and detailed vascular/biliary relationship of the liver lesion – essential to confirm that a non anatomic resection will achieve clear margins without compromising hepatic inflow/outflow.

C. Confirmation of absence of extrahepatic disease on full staging.
D. a chest CT scan

F. Status and symptoms related to the primary colon tumor.

Case_Content:
Man, 62 years old, T3N1M1 upper rectal tumor, liver metastases (3-5 cm) with contact with IVC and right hepatic vein at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 580 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Complex central metastases, discussion on combined approach or venous reconstruction.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
• Category: Potentially resectable  
• Reasoning: The liver lesions are described as 3‑5 cm with contact to the inferior vena cava and the right hepatic vein, indicating major vascular involvement that may require complex venous reconstruction. Critical technical information is missing (exact number of lesions, hepatic segments involved, future liver remnant (FLR) volume, and detailed vascular anatomy from liver MRI). Additionally, the patient’s systemic treatment history and response are unknown, which are needed to judge oncologic feasibility and to potentially downsize the disease. Because a specific prerequisite (pre‑operative high‑resolution liver MRI ± volumetry and/or neoadjuvant chemotherapy to assess response and FLR) is required before a definitive surgical plan can be made, the case falls into the “Potentially resectable” category.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Complete staging work‑up  
   – Obtain a contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with vascular sequences to define the exact number of metastases, segmental distribution, depth of IVC/right hepatic‑vein involvement, and to calculate FLR volume.  
   – Perform molecular profiling of the rectal primary (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MSI/MMR status) to guide systemic therapy and potential targeted agents.  
   – Confirm that the primary rectal tumor has not been resected and assess for obstructive or bleeding symptoms; if present, consider diverting stoma.  

2. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (conversion chemotherapy)  
   – Initiate a doublet regimen (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) ± biologic agent (bevacizumab for RAS‑wild type, anti‑EGFR for RAS‑mutant) for 2–3 months.  
   – Re‑image with MRI after 2 cycles to evaluate tumor shrinkage, especially at the vascular interface, and to reassess FLR.  

3. Decision point after chemotherapy  
   – If adequate response (≥30 % reduction of lesion size, improved vascular clearance) and FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % in steatotic liver), proceed to a liver‑first (reverse) approach:  
        a. Portal vein embolization (PVE) of the right portal territory if FLR is borderline.  
        b. Planned major right hepatectomy with IVC/right hepatic‑vein reconstruction (using autologous graft or prosthetic conduit) performed by an experienced HPB team.  
   – If response is insufficient or FLR remains inadequate, consider a two‑stage hepatectomy (left‑lateral resection first, then hypertrophy interval, followed by right‑sided resection) or add ablative techniques.  

4. Management of the rectal primary  
   – After hepatic surgery and recovery (≈4–6 weeks), deliver long‑course chemoradiotherapy (CRT) for the upper rectal tumor (if not already given) as per TNT protocols.  
   – Restage the rectal tumor with pelvic MRI; if still resectable, perform total mesorectal excision (TME) with clear circumferential margins.  
   – Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (continuation of the pre‑operative regimen) to complete a total of 6 months of systemic therapy.  

5. Surveillance  
   – Serial CEA measurements and cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–4 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months thereafter.  

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
- Precise FLR ratio (volumetric assessment) to determine safety of major hepatectomy.  
- Detailed liver MRI findings: number of metastases, exact hepatic segments involved, depth of IVC/right hepatic‑vein invasion, arterial anatomy.  
- Systemic treatment history and current response (has any chemotherapy been given, and what was the radiologic/CEA response?).  
- Molecular phenotype of the primary tumor (KRAS/NRAS/BRAF/MSI) to select appropriate systemic agents.  
- Status of the primary rectal tumor (resected vs intact, presence of obstruction/bleeding) to decide on need for diversion or immediate local therapy.  

These pieces of information are required to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.

Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with centrally located liver metastases (3–5 cm) in contact with the IVC and the right hepatic vein in the setting of an upper rectal T3N1 tumor, without reported extrahepatic disease. Although the number of lesions is not specified as excessive, the venous involvement makes a standard parenchymal-sparing R0 resection unsafe without complex vascular control or reconstruction. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable only after tumor downsizing and expert HPB / vascular reassessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver and pelvis MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships.
• Given the high CEA level (580 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Mandatory induction systemic therapy
• Initiate 2–3 months of induction chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).
• The objective is tumor downsizing and reduction of venous contact.

• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Multidisciplinary evaluation with complex surgery to assess feasibility of venous reconstruction if required or right hepatomy including en-bloc resection of the right hepatic vein according to the future liver remnant.

D. Surgical management if feasibility is confirmed
• If regression occurs or venous reconstruction is deemed feasible, plan an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resection with the aim of R0 margin.
• Anticipate possible IVC and/or hepatic vein reconstruction.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential.

E. Surgical management after restaging : management of the rectal primary (oncologic priority)
• Given the T3N1 rectal cancer, long-course radiotherapy is appropriate to optimize local control and allow coordinated surgical planning 
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvis MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : with strict follow up of primary tumor
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery, using a staged or synchronous strategy : oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles).
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.

E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging every 3 months.
