• Continue systemic and targeted therapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented management according to MDT.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Precise extent and depth of contact with the IVC and right hepatic vein on MRI.
B. Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge, and circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI influencing surgical approach and anastomotic risk
C. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of the three liver lesions on MRI.
D. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
E. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy and long-course pelvic radiotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA
F. Patient’s nutritional status and postoperative recovery capacity, relevant for timing of chemotherapy.
G. Trend and quantification of circulating tumor cells over time.

Case_Content:
Woman, 67 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer, multiple liver metastases at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan and normal CEA at 3 ng/mL. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Biological discordance, question regarding the utility of CEA follow-up in this profile.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – The case lacks decisive technical and biological information required to confirm that an R0 liver resection can be performed now. Specifically, the primary colon tumour has not been reported as resected, the number, size, segmental distribution and vascular/biliary involvement of the liver lesions are missing, and the future liver remnant (FLR) ratio has not been calculated. Because these missing items directly determine whether a safe, margin‑negative hepatectomy is feasible, the patient must first undergo further evaluation and likely down‑staging before surgery can be planned.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Confirm staging and biology  
  – Obtain a contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to define lesion number, size, bilobar vs unilobar distribution, vascular contact and to calculate FLR.  
  – Complete brain imaging (MRI) to rule out occult brain metastasis (the only extra‑hepatic site still listed as Missing).  
  – Verify that the primary tumour has been resected; if not, plan resection of the right‑sided colon cancer (simultaneous with liver surgery if feasible, otherwise staged).  

• Systemic induction therapy  
  – Initiate intensive neoadjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab) because the tumour is KRAS‑mutated, right‑sided, T4N2 and likely presents with synchronous, multiple liver metastases – a profile associated with poorer biology and a high likelihood of needing tumour shrinkage before resection.  
  – Re‑image after 2–3 months of chemotherapy to assess radiologic response and to re‑calculate FLR.  

• Functional optimisation  
  – If FLR is projected <20‑30 % after expected tumour shrinkage, schedule portal vein embolisation (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy.  

• Surgical plan (once resectability confirmed)  
  – If the primary tumour is asymptomatic after systemic therapy, adopt a “liver‑first” approach: perform curative‑intent hepatectomy (anatomical or parenchymal‑sparing) aiming for R0 margins, preserving ≥30 % functional liver volume.  
  – If the primary tumour is symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding) or if simultaneous resection is technically feasible, perform combined colon resection and hepatectomy in a single operation.  
  – Consider adjunctive thermal ablation or stereotactic body radiotherapy for lesions that remain unresectable after downsizing.  

• Post‑operative management  
  – Continue adjuvant systemic therapy (e.g., continuation of the same regimen or switch to maintenance biologic) for at least 6 months, guided by response and tolerability.  
  – Enroll in regular surveillance: CEA (though low, still useful), CT chest/abdomen every 3–6 months, and MRI liver annually.  

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
- Status of the primary colorectal tumour (resected vs pending).  
- Detailed liver metastasis characteristics: number of lesions, maximum diameter, hepatic segments involved, presence of vascular or biliary invasion.  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio or volumetry.  
- Timing of liver metastases (synchronous vs metachronous).  
- Whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been administered.  
- Results of liver MRI (including hepatobiliary contrast) and any portal vein embolisation planning.  
- Brain imaging results (to exclude occult brain metastasis).

From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable after major conversion. • Perform right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis

• Complete a total of approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.

• Imaging-based surveillance is essential, as CEA is not a reliable marker in this patient.

B. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy (decrease, stability or progression)

Case_Content:
Man, 58 years old, left T3N1M1 colon cancer, bilobar metastases (1.5-3 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 400 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, POLE mutation detected.
MDT Discussion: Hypermutated profile, rare, may justify immunotherapy in some strategies.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – the liver lesions are small (1.5‑3 cm) and bilobar, suggesting that a parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy could be technically feasible. However decisive information is missing: a liver‑specific MRI to define the exact number of metastases, segmental distribution, vascular or biliary involvement, and a calculated future liver remnant (FLR) ratio. Without these data the surgeon cannot confirm that an R0 resection preserving ≥30 % FLR (or ≥40 % in a steatotic liver) is possible, nor can the need for portal vein embolisation or a two‑stage approach be ruled out. In addition, the primary tumour has not yet been resected and its symptom status is unknown, which influences the choice between simultaneous versus staged surgery. Therefore the case is classified as “Potentially resectable”.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Initial multidisciplinary discussion (colorectal surgeon, hepatobiliary surgeon, medical oncologist, radiologist).  
• Obtain a high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast and calculate the FLR volume.  
• If FLR is adequate and no major vascular/biliary invasion is seen, proceed to neoadjuvant systemic therapy to (a) assess tumour biology, (b) lower the CEA (currently 400 ng/mL), and (c) potentially down‑size any borderline lesions.  
   – Preferred regimen: oxaliplatin‑based doublet (e.g., FOLFOX) combined with an anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab) because the tumour is RAS‑wild‑type; consider adding a checkpoint inhibitor if the POLE mutation is associated with ultra‑high TMB and the tumour is MSI‑high (test for MMR status).  
   – Give 4–6 cycles; restage with repeat CT and MRI after cycle 3 and at completion.  
• Re‑assessment of resectability after chemotherapy:  
   – If FLR remains insufficient, consider portal vein embolisation (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy (first stage: clearance of lesions in one lobe, PVE, then second‑stage resection).  
   – If disease is stable or responding and FLR is adequate, plan a liver‑first approach: parenchymal‑sparing resection of all visible metastases (aim for R0, ≤1 mm margin).  
• After hepatic surgery, address the primary colon tumour:  
   – If the primary is asymptomatic and the patient recovers well, perform a laparoscopic left‑colectomy 4–6 weeks later (sequential strategy).  
   – If the primary is symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding) or if intra‑operative assessment deems it safe, a simultaneous resection can be considered.  
• Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (same regimen as neoadjuvant) for 3–6 months, adjusted for postoperative recovery.  
• Enroll the patient in a clinical trial evaluating immunotherapy for POLE‑mutated, hyper‑mutated CRC if available.  
• Long‑term surveillance: CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of chest/abdomen every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

Step 3 – Missing data  
• Liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast (to define number, exact segmental location, vascular/biliary involvement).  
• Calculated future liver remnant (FLR) ratio.  
• Exact count of hepatic metastases and their distribution across segments.  
• Presence or absence of symptoms from the primary tumour (obstruction, perforation, bleeding).  
• Status of primary tumour resection (has it been performed or not).  
• Results of MMR/MSI testing to confirm whether the POLE mutation confers a hyper‑mutated phenotype amenable to checkpoint inhibition.  
These missing items are essential to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.

Case_Content:
Woman, 69 years old, T4N2M1 transverse colon cancer, seven liver metastases at the abdominal CT scan, CEA 1150 ng/mL, NRAS Q61R mutation.
MDT Discussion: Specific NRAS molecular profile, no sensitivity to anti-EGFR.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: the case lacks decisive information required to judge technical feasibility (future liver remnant volume, hepatic segment distribution, lesion size, vascular/biliary involvement) and there is no record of prior systemic therapy that could downsize the disease. Both a prerequisite conversion chemotherapy and completion of missing imaging/volumetric data are needed before a definitive surgical plan can be made.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Complete staging: obtain a high‑quality contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or Gd‑EOB‑MRI) and a thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to confirm the absence of extra‑hepatic disease and to define lesion size, segmental distribution, and vascular contact.  
- Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR) volume; if FLR < 30 % (or < 40 % in a 69‑year‑old), plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy.  
- Initiate conversion systemic therapy because of RAS mutation and lack of anti‑EGFR sensitivity: oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX) combined with bevacizumab, for 3–4 cycles (or up to 6 cycles if tolerated). Monitor CEA trend; a falling CEA supports tumor responsiveness.  
- Re‑image after chemotherapy (MRI) to assess radiologic response, re‑calculate FLR, and determine whether all hepatic lesions can be resected with negative margins while preserving at least two contiguous liver segments and adequate inflow/outflow.  
- If response is adequate and FLR is sufficient, proceed to curative‑intent liver resection (single‑stage if FLR acceptable, otherwise staged approach after PVE or ALPPS). Aim for R0 resection of all metastases.  
- Address the primary transverse colon tumor: if the patient is asymptomatic, the colon resection can be performed simultaneously with the liver operation or in a second staged procedure after hepatic clearance; if obstructive, bleeding or perforated, manage urgently (endoscopic stent, diverting colostomy, or immediate colectomy) before or during the hepatic surgery.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy: resume the same regimen (FOLFOX + bevacizumab) for a total of 6 months, provided postoperative recovery is adequate and no contraindications arise.  
- Follow‑up: serial CEA, imaging at 3‑month intervals for the first year, then every 6 months, to detect recurrence early.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio and volumetric assessment.  
- Detailed hepatic lesion characteristics: maximum/minimum diameter, segmental involvement, vascular or biliary contact.  
- Results of liver MRI (or equivalent high‑resolution imaging).  
- Thoracic imaging to exclude pulmonary metastases.  
- Status of the primary tumor (resected or not, presence of obstruction, perforation, bleeding).  
- Whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been administered.  
These items are essential to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.

From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered unresectable.

• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships of all lesions.
• Given the high CEA level (1150 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

• The NRAS Q61R mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.

• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 2–3 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

• Surgical re-evaluation could be considered only if a major radiologic and biologic response occurs with significant reduction in number and size of lesions allowing parenchymal-sparing resections with R0 margin.

E. Management of primary tumor
• If symptomatic or if consideration of intra arterial chemotherapy, perform extended right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right and transverse colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

G. If disease remains extensive
• Continue systemic therapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented management according to MDT.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Precise relationship of each lesion to the hepatic vein confluence on MRI.
B. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of the three lesions.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Confirmation of absence of extrahepatic disease on full staging.
E. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
F. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy and long-course pelvic radiotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA
G. Patient’s nutritional status and postoperative recovery capacity, relevant for timing of chemotherapy.

Case_Content:
Man, 70 years old, left colon tumor, three liver metastases at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 200 ng/mL, RAS wild-type, MSS. MRI: invasion of the hepatic vein confluence.
MDT Discussion: Superior vascular involvement, significant technical risk, volume to be assessed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- The MRI shows invasion of the hepatic‑vein confluence, indicating major vascular involvement that may preclude a margin‑negative (R0) resection without complex reconstruction.  
- Technical resectability cannot be confirmed because the future‑liver‑remnant (FLR) ratio is missing; adequate FLR (>20‑30 % of standardized liver volume) is essential, especially when a major hepatectomy or venous reconstruction is contemplated.  
- Therefore a prerequisite step (volumetric assessment ± portal‑vein embolization or staged approach) is required before definitive surgery can be planned.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Induction systemic therapy: start a RAS‑wild‑type–directed regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± anti‑EGFR antibody) for 2–3 months to (a) assess tumor biology (“proof of time”), (b) attempt downsizing of the hepatic lesions, and (c) treat any occult micrometastatic disease.  
- Re‑assessment after induction: repeat high‑quality liver‑specific MRI (including hepatobiliary contrast) and thin‑slice CT to (i) measure lesion size, (ii) delineate the exact extent of hepatic‑vein involvement, (iii) calculate FLR volume, and (iv) evaluate arterial and biliary anatomy.  
- If FLR is insufficient: perform portal‑vein embolization (PVE) or consider a two‑stage hepatectomy/ALPPS to induce hypertrophy of the remnant.  
- Surgical sequencing:  
   1. Liver‑first approach (preferred) – once adequate FLR and acceptable vascular anatomy are confirmed, proceed with curative‑intent hepatic resection, including hepatic‑vein reconstruction if needed, aiming for R0 margins.  
   2. Primary‑tumor management – after hepatic resection (or concurrently if the colon lesion is asymptomatic and patient fitness allows), perform definitive left‑colon resection (segmental colectomy or extended resection) with oncologic lymph‑node clearance.  
- Adjuvant therapy: complete the planned postoperative chemotherapy (same regimen or adapted based on response) for a total of 6‑12 months, given the synchronous presentation and high CEA (200 ng/mL).  

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
- Future‑liver‑remnant (FLR) ratio / volumetric data.  
- Exact size of each liver metastasis and the hepatic segments involved.  
- Detailed description of the hepatic‑vein invasion (length, circumferential involvement) and arterial anatomy.  
- Status of the primary colorectal tumor (resected or not, presence of obstruction/bleeding/perforation).  
- Grade of differentiation of the primary tumor and any lymph‑node involvement.  
- Baseline liver function / presence of steatosis or fibrosis that could affect postoperative liver reserve.  
- Evaluation for occult extra‑hepatic disease (e.g., brain MRI, PET‑CT) that was not performed.  

These items must be obtained before the definitive surgical plan can be finalized.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with three liver metastases and MRI evidence of invasion of the hepatic vein confluence, without reported extrahepatic disease. Although the number of lesions is limited, involvement of the venous outflow confluence makes a safe R0 resection with preservation of adequate hepatic venous drainage technically uncertain at this stage. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable only after tumor downsizing and expert vascular reassessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships of all lesions and a chest CT scan
• Given the high CEA level (200 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Mandatory induction systemic therapy
• Initiate 2–3 months of induction chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status).
• The objective is tumor downsizing and potential reduction of venous involvement.

C. Radiologic reassessment after treatment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 2-3 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

D. Expert HPB/vascular and volumetric restaging
• Repeat high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of lesions to the hepatic vein confluence.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR) and evaluate feasibility of venous preservation or need for reconstruction.

E. Surgical management if feasibility is confirmed
• If significant regression occurs, plan an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resection with the aim of R0 margin.
• Anticipate possible venous reconstruction or complex vascular control.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential.

F. Management of primary tumor
• If symptomatic or if consideration of intra arterial chemotherapy, perform left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.

G. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

B. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of the three lesions.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Confirmation of absence of extrahepatic disease on full staging.
E. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy

Case_Content:
Woman, 56 years old, right T3N1M1 colon cancer, four liver metastases (3-5 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 780 ng/mL, non-V600E BRAF mutation (D594G).
MDT Discussion: Atypical BRAF mutation, intermediate prognosis, bilobar liver involvement.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has four bilobar liver metastases (3‑5 cm) and no radiologically evident extra‑hepatic disease, which technically could be resected if an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved. However, the structured analysis lacks two decisive pieces of information: (a) FLR ratio compatibility with surgery (FLR % required ≥ 30 % in a normal liver or ≥ 40 % after chemotherapy‑induced injury) and (b) whether the primary colon tumour has already been resected (or if it requires simultaneous or staged resection). Both items are essential to confirm that a margin‑negative (R0) hepatectomy is feasible without compromising postoperative liver function. Until these data are obtained, the case must be considered potentially resectable, with neoadjuvant therapy and further imaging to clarify technical feasibility.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Initiate systemic therapy aimed at tumour down‑staging and biological selection: 6 cycles of a fluoropyrimidine‑oxaliplatin doublet (FOLFOX) combined with bevacizumab, which is the preferred regimen for BRAF‑mutated (non‑V600E) mCRC and avoids anti‑EGFR agents that are ineffective in this molecular context.  
• Restage after chemotherapy with a high‑resolution liver MRI (including diffusion‑weighted and hepatocyte‑specific contrast sequences) and repeat CT‑based volumetry to (i) assess radiologic response of each lesion, (ii) delineate the hepatic segments involved, (iii) evaluate vascular or biliary encroachment, and (iv) calculate the FLR ratio.  
• If FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % after chemotherapy) and all lesions can be cleared with negative margins, proceed to curative‑intent liver surgery. For bilobar disease, a staged “liver‑first” approach is advisable:  
 – Stage 1: portal vein embolization (PVE) of the liver sector that will be resected if FLR is borderline, followed by resection of the dominant lobe (e.g., right hepatectomy) after hypertrophy.  
 – Stage 2 (4–6 weeks later): completion hepatectomy of the contralateral lesions (e.g., left lateral resection or non‑anatomic resections) to achieve R0 status.  
• If the primary tumour has not yet been removed and is asymptomatic, schedule a right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection with adequate lymphadenectomy) after hepatic surgery, allowing recovery of liver function before bowel surgery (or perform simultaneous resection only if intra‑operative assessment confirms safe liver remnant).  
• Post‑operative (adjuvant) systemic therapy: resume FOLFOX ± bevacizumab for a total of 6 months, adjusting based on postoperative pathology and tolerance.  
• Enrolment in a clinical trial targeting BRAF‑mutated colorectal cancer (e.g., combination of a BRAF inhibitor with EGFR/MEK blockade) should be considered, given the intermediate prognosis associated with the D594G mutation.  

Step 3 – Missing data (most crucial for decision‑making)  
• FLR ratio compatibility with surgery (volumetric assessment).  
• Status of the primary colon tumour (resected vs. pending).  
• Detailed hepatic segment involvement and presence/absence of vascular or biliary contact/invasion.  
• Timing of liver metastases (synchronous vs. metachronous) to refine biological risk.  
• Availability of a liver‑specific MRI to complete morphologic assessment.  
• Whether any systemic therapy has already been administered (to gauge chemotherapy‑induced liver injury).  
These items must be obtained before a definitive surgical plan can be finalized.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with four bilobar liver metastases (3–5 cm) in the setting of a right T3N1 colon cancer and elevated CEA (780 ng/mL). Despite bilobar distribution, the limited number of lesions suggests that parenchymal-sparing resections could achieve R0 margins while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. The presence of a non-V600E BRAF D594G mutation is associated with a more indolent biology compared with V600E and does not contraindicate surgical intent. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships of all lesions.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Short peri-operative systemic therapy (recommended)
• Given the high CEA and bilobar disease, administer 2–3 months of induction chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).
• The objective is treatment of micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Radiologic reassessment after treatment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 2-3 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

D. Surgical management after restaging
• If disease remains controlled, perform ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resections of all four lesions.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to optimize margins and preserve parenchyma.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

E. Management of primary tumor
• Perform right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon cancer) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for colectomy.

F. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of the four lesions.
B. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
C. Patient’s performance status and comorbidities.
D. Confirmation of absence of extrahepatic disease on full staging.
E. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
F. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy and long-course pelvic radiotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA
G. Patient’s nutritional status and postoperative recovery capacity, relevant for timing of chemotherapy.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Man, 65 years old, left T4N2M1 colon cancer, six liver metastases (2-4 cm)at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 320 ng/mL, RAS wild-type, MSS. Positive circulating tumor cells detected.
MDT Discussion: Presence of circulating tumor cells despite no visible extension, prognostic value discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: The case reports six liver metastases (2‑4 cm) but lacks critical anatomic information required to confirm technical feasibility – namely the hepatic segments involved, presence of vascular or biliary contact, and a volumetric assessment of the future liver remnant (FLR). Additionally, the primary colon tumor has not been reported as resected, and the timing of the liver disease (synchronous vs metachronous) is unknown. Because these missing items are decisive for surgical planning, the disease cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront”. No absolute contraindication (e.g., extra‑hepatic disease, uncontrolled progression) is present, so the case is not “Not resectable”. The need for further imaging, FLR calculation, and likely neoadjuvant systemic therapy makes it “Potentially resectable”.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Confirm primary tumor status – obtain operative report or imaging to determine whether the left‑sided T4N2 primary has already been resected; if not, plan for curative‑intent colectomy (either staged before liver surgery or simultaneous if intra‑operative assessment permits).  
2. Complete hepatic staging – perform a contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with hepatobiliary‑specific agent and three‑dimensional volumetry to define:  
   - exact segmental distribution of the six lesions,  
   - relationship to major hepatic vessels and biliary structures,  
   - calculate FLR; if FLR < 30 % (or < 40 % in patients with chemotherapy‑associated liver injury) plan portal vein embolisation (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy.  
3. Systemic conversion therapy – initiate a RAS‑wild‑type‑directed regimen, e.g., 6 cycles of mFOLFOX6 + cetuximab (or FOLFOX + bevacizumab if EGFR contraindicated). High CEA (320 ng/mL) and circulating tumor cells suggest aggressive biology; therefore, neoadjuvant chemotherapy provides both tumor down‑staging and a “test of time” for disease biology.  
4. Re‑assessment after chemotherapy – repeat CT/MRI and CEA; evaluate radiologic response (RECIST) and CTC status. If disease is stable or responding and FLR is adequate, proceed to curative liver surgery.  
5. Surgical plan – aim for R0 resection of all hepatic lesions, preserving at least two contiguous liver segments with adequate inflow/outflow and biliary drainage. Options include:  
   - Single‑stage major hepatectomy if FLR sufficient,  
   - Two‑stage hepatectomy (resection of lesions in one lobe, PVE, then completion hepatectomy), or  
   - Associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) only in highly selected cases.  
6. Post‑operative management – resume the same systemic regimen for 4–6 months as adjuvant therapy, monitor CEA and imaging every 3–4 months for the first two years.  
7. Multidisciplinary follow‑up – continuous MDT review to address any emerging extra‑hepatic disease (e.g., brain lesions) and to adjust systemic therapy based on molecular or clinical evolution.

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio – determines whether a safe hepatectomy is possible or if PVE/ staged approach is required.  
- Hepatic segment involvement and vascular/biliary anatomy – essential for planning the extent of resection and need for vascular reconstruction.  
- Liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast – provides the detailed lesion mapping and volumetry absent from the current CT assessment.  
- Status of the primary colon tumor (resected vs not) – influences timing of colectomy relative to liver surgery.  
- Timing of liver metastases (synchronous vs metachronous) – impacts the urgency of systemic therapy and surgical sequencing.  
- Whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been administered – affects liver parenchymal quality and choice of further regimen.  
- Extra‑hepatic brain involvement (currently missing) – would alter the overall curative intent if present.

The patient presents with six liver metastases (2–4 cm) without reported extrahepatic disease. Despite the bilobar distribution, the number and size of lesions suggest that parenchymal-sparing resections could achieve R0 margins while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. The detection of circulating tumor cells reflects increased systemic risk but does not alter technical resectability. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable.

A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships and calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Mandatory peri-operative systemic therapy
• Given the presence of circulating tumor cells indicating systemic dissemination risk, administer 2–3 months of induction chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status).
• The objective is treatment of micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Radiologic reassessment after treatment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 2-3 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

D. Surgical management after restaging
• If disease remains controlled, perform ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resections of all six lesions.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential.

E. Management of primary tumor
• If symptomatic or if consideration of intra arterial chemotherapy, perform left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.

F. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

B. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of the three liver lesions on MRI.
